questions.question: What is the gospel, in plain words?
questions.shortAnswer: The gospel is the announcement that God has acted to rescue people who could not rescue themselves, through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus. It is news before it is advice.
questions.answer:
The word gospel means good news. Not good advice, not a set of rules to try harder at, but news about something that has already happened. That distinction is the whole game. Advice tells you what to do. News tells you what has been done. The Christian message is news first, and only then does it ask anything of you.

The oldest summary of it is older than the New Testament books that contain it. In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul hands on a creed he himself received, almost certainly within a few years of the crucifixion: that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures. Before there was a cathedral or a denomination, there was that. God entered the world he made, in a man named Jesus, lived the life we failed to live, died the death our sin had earned, and rose again, breaking the power of death itself.

That last clause is not a flourish. If Jesus stayed dead, the gospel is a beautiful lie and Paul says so plainly. But if he rose, then a door has been opened in the wall of death that every human being is walking toward, and the news is that you may go through it.

Notice what this does to religion. Religion is a ladder. Do more, sin less, climb higher, and perhaps God will be pleased. The gospel cuts the ladder down. It says the climbing was never going to reach, and that God came down the ladder to you. J. Gresham Machen put it sharply a century ago: Christianity is not a life, it is first a doctrine, an account of something that occurred. The new life follows the news. It does not produce it.

This is why grace offends respectable people more than it offends obvious sinners. The sinner knows he needs a gift. The respectable man wants a wage, and the gospel does not pay wages for righteousness, because none of us has earned one. You are accepted on the strength of what Jesus did, not on the strength of your performance, which means you can stop auditioning.

The right response to news is not effort. It is trust. You hear what God has done, you stop trying to save yourself, and you put your weight on Jesus the way you put your weight on a chair you trust to hold you. God came to get us. Everything else in the Christian life grows out of that one root.

questions.question: Can I lose my salvation?
questions.shortAnswer: Faithful Christians genuinely disagree on this. Some hold that a true believer is kept secure by God forever, and others hold that a person can finally walk away from faith.
questions.answer:
Few questions cause more anxious nights than this one, and the anxiety usually comes from confusing two different things: whether you are secure in Christ, and whether a given person who once professed faith was ever truly in him. The Bible speaks to both, and Christians have long divided over how to fit them.

On one side stand the passages of staggering security. Jesus says his sheep will never perish and no one can snatch them from his hand. Paul says he is convinced that nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God in Christ, and that the One who began a good work will complete it. This stream, sometimes called the perseverance of the saints, insists that salvation is God's work from start to finish, and that a work God begins, God finishes. Your security does not rest on the strength of your grip on him but on the strength of his grip on you.

On the other side stand the sober warnings, the branches that do not abide and are cut off, the people who fall away, the exhortations to hold fast and not drift. The Wesleyan and Arminian traditions read these as real warnings about a real possibility, that a person can finally refuse the grace they once received. They fear that a doctrine of unconditional security can lull people into presuming on grace while living as though Christ were nothing to them.

Here is the pastoral wisdom underneath the debate, which both sides largely share in practice. The New Testament also describes people who walked away and shows that their leaving revealed they had never truly belonged, they went out from us because they were not of us. So genuine faith perseveres, and a faith that finally and permanently abandons Christ shows what it always was. Either way, the warnings are not noise. They are one of the means God uses to keep his people walking.

So what do you do with the fear. You do not resolve it by introspection, endlessly inspecting your own sincerity, which only feeds the anxiety. You resolve it by looking to Christ. Assurance is not found by staring at the strength of your faith but at the object of it. If you are worried you have wandered too far, the very worry is a pull homeward, and the arms are open. Run to him. That motion, not a theory about security, is what a living faith looks like.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Reformed Christians hold to the perseverance of the saints, that the truly saved are kept secure forever, while Arminian and Wesleyan Christians hold that a person can finally and freely turn away from faith.

questions.question: How can I know I am really saved?
questions.shortAnswer: Assurance rests mainly on what Christ has done and promised, not on the temperature of your feelings, though a changing life and an inward witness can confirm it over time.
questions.answer:
How can I know I am really saved is one of the most common questions sincere Christians ask, and the anxiety behind it is usually a good sign, not a bad one. The careless rarely worry. It is the people who take God seriously who lie awake wondering if it took.

The first thing to say is where assurance does not come from. It does not come from the intensity of your feelings, which rise and fall with sleep and weather and brain chemistry. It does not come from a flawless record, because if your standing depended on that none of us would have it. And it does not come from the vividness of a past moment, the date on a card, because some who can name the day have no fruit, and some who cannot remember a moment have walked with Christ for fifty years.

The Bible points to three grounds instead, and they work together. The first and deepest is the finished work of Christ and the promises attached to it. Assurance is found by looking out at him, not in at yourself. He said whoever comes to him he will never cast out, and your security rests on his faithfulness, not the steadiness of your grip. The second is the inner witness of the Spirit, who testifies with our spirit that we are God's children, the deep settled sense, often quiet, that you belong to him and may call him Father. The third is the evidence of a changed life, not perfection but direction, a new love for God and his people, a grief over sin you once excused, a slow real movement toward holiness. John wrote his first letter precisely so believers would know, and he pointed to all three: the truth about Christ, the Spirit, and a life that shows it.

Notice the danger of leaning on only one. Lean only on a past decision and you may presume while living as though Christ were nothing. Lean only on present fruit and you will despair on every bad day. Lean only on feelings and you will be at the mercy of your moods. Held together, they give a sturdy, honest assurance.

So if you are anxious tonight, do not resolve it by staring harder at the quality of your own faith, which only feeds the fear. Resolve it by looking to the One your faith is resting on. Then keep walking with him. A living thing grows, and the growth itself, over time, becomes part of the answer.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ in emphasis, with some grounding assurance chiefly in Christ's objective promise and others looking also to the inward witness of the Spirit and the evidence of a changed life.

questions.question: Do I have to be good enough for God to accept me?
questions.shortAnswer: No. The heart of the Christian message is that God accepts you on the basis of Christ's goodness, not yours, and the goodness then grows out of being accepted.
questions.answer:
Do I have to be good enough for God to accept me is the question almost everyone brings to religion, and it contains a hidden assumption that the gospel exists to overturn. The assumption is that acceptance is a wage you earn by performance. Christianity says, bluntly, that you will never be good enough, and then says that this is not the bad news you fear. It is the doorway to the only good news there is.

Every other religion and most of irreligion runs on the same engine: behave, perform, achieve, and then you will be accepted, by God or by your own conscience or by the people whose approval you crave. It produces two kinds of people and no others. Those who think they are succeeding become proud and hard. Those who know they are failing become anxious and crushed. Either way the self is on trial and the verdict is never finally in.

The gospel turns the order around. It does not say behave and then be accepted. It says you are accepted, on the strength of what Christ did, and now you may behave out of gratitude rather than fear. Acceptance is the root, not the reward. The theologians call this justification, being declared right with God as a gift, received by faith and not earned by works, so that no one can boast. You are loved before you are good, which is the only thing that has ever actually made anyone good.

This is why grace is so hard for respectable people to swallow. The obvious sinner knows he needs a gift. The diligent rule-keeper wants a wage, and resents a God who pays the latecomer the same as the man who worked all day. But God does not run a payroll for righteousness. He runs a household, and he adopts.

So no, you do not have to be good enough, and the relief of that is meant to go all the way down. You can stop auditioning for a part you already have. The pressure to prove yourself, to God and to everyone else, can come off, because the verdict you spend your life chasing has already been spoken over you in Christ. That, and not your performance, is the ground you stand on.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Protestants and Catholics frame the relationship between faith and works differently, yet both deny that you earn God's love and both affirm that genuine faith bears fruit.

questions.question: Do I really have to go to church?
questions.shortAnswer: You are not saved by attendance, but the Christian life was never meant to be lived alone, and gathering with other believers is one of the chief means God uses to hold and grow you.
questions.answer:
Plenty of people who love God carry real wounds from church, so this question often is not lazy. It is honest, and sometimes it is grief. Take that seriously before you take the answer.

Going to church does not earn your standing with God. You are accepted in Christ whether or not you show up on a given Sunday. So in that narrow sense, no, your salvation does not hang on attendance.

And yet the New Testament never imagines a solitary Christian. From the start, to belong to Christ was to belong to his people, a body where each part needs the others. You were made to be known, corrected, carried, and fed in a way that is nearly impossible alone, and the church, for all its failures, is where that ordinarily happens. The instruction not to neglect meeting together is not about filling seats. It is about not trying to survive a hard road by yourself.

So the better question is not whether you have to, but whether you will let yourself be helped. Find a community that handles Scripture honestly and treats people like people. Go not to be inspected, but to belong.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on church government and exactly what a healthy congregation looks like, but across traditions they agree that belonging to a local body is normal and good for the believer, not optional decoration.

questions.question: Why pray if God already knows everything?
questions.shortAnswer: Prayer is less about informing God and more about being with him, and the Bible teaches that God genuinely chooses to work through the prayers of his people.
questions.answer:
If God already knows everything and has already decided what is best, prayer can feel pointless, like writing letters to someone who has read them before you sent them. The puzzle is real, and the Bible answers it less by solving the riddle than by reframing what prayer is for.

First, prayer is mainly about relationship, not information. You do not tell your closest friend things to update their database. You tell them because that is what love does, it shares life. Jesus said your Father knows what you need before you ask, and then in the next breath taught his followers to ask anyway. The asking is not for God's benefit. It is the form intimacy takes. A child who only spoke to a parent to extract things would not have a relationship, just a vending machine.

Second, and more surprising, the Bible presents prayer as something God genuinely uses to accomplish his will, not a workaround of it. He ordains the ends and he ordains the means, and prayer is one of the means. Scripture can say you have not because you ask not, and can show God responding to the prayers of his people, without implying he was caught off guard. A good father plans to give his children many things precisely through their asking, because the asking is part of the good he intends, drawing them to depend on him. Prayer changes things in part by changing us into people who depend.

Third, prayer is how we are slowly remade. In honest prayer we stop performing, name what is really happening, and align ourselves with God rather than trying to bend him to us. The deepest prayer is not getting God to do my will but coming to want his, the prayer Jesus prayed in the garden, not my will but yours. That is not resignation. It is the hardest and freest thing a human being can say.

So pray, even with the philosophical puzzle unresolved, because the puzzle assumes prayer is a mechanism for getting outcomes, and it is first a way of being with God. He is not a force to be operated. He is a Father to be known, and prayer is the conversation in which the knowing happens.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians hold differing accounts of how prayer and God's sovereign plan fit together, yet all the major streams affirm both that God knows all things and that he truly invites and responds to prayer.

questions.question: How should Christians treat people who disagree with them?
questions.shortAnswer: With honesty about the disagreement and unmistakable love toward the person, holding conviction and kindness together rather than trading one for the other.
questions.answer:
The temptation runs in two directions. One is to win at any cost, treating the person on the other side as an enemy to be beaten. The other is to keep the peace by pretending nothing is at stake. Jesus refused both. He was full of grace and full of truth at once, and he did not split the difference.

Start with the dignity of the other person. Whoever disagrees with you, however sharply, is someone made in the image of God and someone Christ died for. That does not vanish when they are wrong. Paul tells us to speak the truth, and in the same breath to do it in love, because truth delivered as a weapon stops being a witness.

This includes disagreement among Christians. On the central things, the church should be clear. On the many secondary things, where godly believers read the same Bible and reach different conclusions, the older wisdom holds. Unity in essentials, freedom in non-essentials, and in all things love.

The hardest test is the person who will not extend you the same grace. The Christian standard does not wait for the other side to earn it. You answer with patience and respect first, not because they deserve it, but because that is the One you follow. People will know whose you are less by your arguments than by how you treat the people you argue with.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians draw the line differently between essential matters worth dividing over and secondary matters that call for forbearance, which is one reason humility about your own placement of that line is itself part of charity.

questions.question: Why does God allow suffering and evil?
questions.shortAnswer: The Bible never treats suffering as a tidy problem to be solved, and neither will we. It refuses easy explanation and instead points to a God who entered the suffering himself rather than explaining it from a distance.
questions.answer:
This is the oldest objection there is, and it deserves to be stated at full strength before any answer is attempted. Epicurus framed it three centuries before Christ: if God is willing to prevent evil but not able, he is not all-powerful; if able but not willing, he is not all-good; if both able and willing, where does evil come from. A faith that cannot sit in that room honestly is not worth defending.

Start with what Christianity does not say. It does not say suffering is an illusion, as some Eastern philosophies do. It does not say the material world is evil, as the ancient Gnostics did. It does not even say, in the end, that every instance of suffering has a tidy purpose you could understand if you tried hard enough. The book of Job spends thirty-eight chapters refusing exactly that comfort.

What it offers first is the free-will defense, developed in our time by the philosopher Alvin Plantinga. A world of creatures who can genuinely love is a world of creatures who can genuinely refuse, and you cannot have the first without the risk of the second. Much of the worst suffering, the cruelty of people to people, is the price of our not being puppets. Love that cannot be withheld is not love.

But that does not cover the cancer ward or the earthquake, and Christianity does not pretend it does. Here it says something stranger than philosophy. It does not hand you an explanation. It hands you a person. The central image of the faith is not a God safely above the suffering but a God hanging inside it, executed on a Roman cross. C.S. Lewis, who wrote a calm book about pain and then watched his wife die and wrote a furious one, came to rest there. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in a Nazi prison, wrote that only the suffering God can help.

This is the answer that is not an answer. The Christian claim is not that God explains your pain from a distance but that he entered it, that the marks are still on the risen body, and that he has promised to end it, not with a syllogism but with a new creation where he wipes away every tear and death itself dies. Dostoevsky put the protest in the mouth of Ivan Karamazov, who could not accept a heaven bought with one child's tears. The gospel does not refute Ivan. It out-suffers him.

So if you are in it now, you are not being asked to feel that it is fine. You are being invited to bring the anger to the God who has a cross of his own, and to wait, in the dark, for the morning he swore is coming.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how much God ordains versus merely permits, with some emphasizing his sovereign purpose in all things and others emphasizing human and demonic freedom as the source of evil. Both hold that God is good and that evil is real.

questions.question: Why do bad things happen to good people?
questions.shortAnswer: Jesus directly rejected the idea that suffering measures a person's goodness. The tower that fell and the lives it took proved nothing about the ones who died, and he said so plainly.
questions.answer:
Why do bad things happen to good people is the form the problem of suffering takes when it gets personal, and it carries a quiet assumption worth examining before we comfort anyone with it. The assumption is that the good have it coming to them easy, that virtue should buy safety. The Bible both honors the ache behind the question and gently dismantles its premise.

First, the uncomfortable part. Scripture is honest that, measured against the holiness of God, the category of good people is thinner than we like. Not that the distinctions we draw are meaningless, there really are kind people and cruel ones, but that no one stands before God on the strength of being basically decent. When Jesus was told about Galileans murdered by Pilate and people crushed by a falling tower, he refused to say they were worse sinners who got what they deserved. He cut the line between catastrophe and personal guilt that we keep trying to draw. Suffering is not, mostly, a scoreboard.

Second, the book of Job exists precisely for this question, and its answer is not the one we expect. Job is righteous, and he suffers horribly, and his friends insist he must have sinned to deserve it. God's verdict at the end is that the friends, the ones defending the tidy system, were wrong, and Job, who protested that the system did not fit, was right to protest. The Bible refuses the formula that good people are spared and bad people are struck. It lets the mystery stand.

What it offers instead is not an equation but a presence and a promise. The presence is a God who entered the suffering himself, the truly good one, the only one who actually did not have it coming, who suffered the worst of it on a cross. If anyone had the right to ask why do bad things happen to the good, it was him, and he asked it, my God, why have you forsaken me. The promise is that the story is not over, that the account is not closed at the graveside, that there is a resurrection and a final setting-right where every wrong is addressed and every tear is wiped away.

So to the person in it now, the Christian faith does not hand a reason that would make the pain acceptable. It hands a companion who has been there and a horizon beyond the dark. That is less than the explanation we wanted and, in the end, more than it could have given us.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how to read suffering in a believer's life, with some seeing specific divine discipline or formation in it and others seeing mostly the random fallout of a fallen world. Both reject the claim that suffering proves a person deserved it.

questions.question: Why does God feel so silent when I need him?
questions.shortAnswer: The silence of God is one of the most common experiences in the Bible, not one of the rarest. The people closest to God in Scripture are often the ones crying into what feels like an empty sky.
questions.answer:
Why does God feel so silent when I need him most is not a beginner's question. It is the cry of people far along the road, and the Bible takes it so seriously that it gave the experience a permanent place in its songbook. A third of the Psalms are laments, and many of them are addressed to a God who seems to have gone quiet at the worst possible time.

First, name what this is not. The silence is not necessarily a sign of his absence or your failure. Scripture is full of faithful people who endured long stretches of it. The Psalmist asks how long, O Lord, will you forget me forever, and that line is in the Bible as prayer, not as proof of unbelief. There can be a darkness that has nothing to do with sin, a hiddenness God allows for reasons we only sometimes see later.

The great spiritual writers had a name for it, the dark night of the soul, John of the Cross's phrase for a season when the felt comfort of God is withdrawn. Their counsel was surprising. They said this is often not abandonment but a deeper work, God weaning us off the gifts so that we learn to love the Giver, burning away the part of our faith that was really only in it for the warm feelings. A love that only works when it is being rewarded with good feelings is still an immature love. The silence can be the furnace where it grows up.

There is also the staggering fact that Jesus himself entered this exact darkness. On the cross he prayed the opening line of Psalm 22, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me. The Son knew the silence of the Father. Which means that when God feels absent to you, you are not in territory he has never walked. He has been in the dark, and he did not stay there, and the psalm he quoted ends in vindication.

So what do you do in the silence. You do what the Psalmists did. You keep talking even when there is no reply, because prayer addressed to a silent God is still faith, the highest kind. You lean on what you knew to be true when you could feel it, the way you trust the sun is there behind clouds you cannot see through. And you wait, in company if you can find it, for the morning. The God who feels hidden has promised he is not, and the felt absence is not the final word about a Father who once shouted his love from a cross.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on whether seasons of God's felt absence are mainly a refining work he intends or simply the ordinary weather of faith in a broken world. Both affirm that God remains present even when he cannot be felt.

questions.question: How can a loving God send people to hell?
questions.shortAnswer: This is one of the heaviest questions a person can ask, and it deserves more than a slogan. Christians have wrestled hard with it and do not all land in the same place.
questions.answer:
No doctrine costs more to defend than hell, and it should never be defended cheaply or with relish. If anyone speaks of it without grief, they have not understood it. So begin by feeling the weight of the objection. A God of love who consigns people to endless torment looks, on its face, like a contradiction the whole faith should collapse under.

A few things reframe it without dissolving it. The first is that the Bible's images for judgment are varied and often less like a torture chamber than like exclusion, a door shut, an outer darkness, a person finally getting the alone they insisted on. C.S. Lewis put it memorably: the gates of hell are locked from the inside. On this reading hell is not God overpowering people who longed for him, but God honoring, at last, the refusal of people who spent a lifetime saying leave me alone. Love that cannot finally be refused is not love. It is coercion.

The second is that we want judgment more than we admit. Confronted with the slave trader, the abuser, the architect of genocide, the human heart cries out that this must not be allowed to stand forever, that there must be a reckoning. The same justice we demand for the world's monsters is the justice that unsettles us when we turn it on ourselves. A God who shrugged at evil, who let every cruelty pass with no final accounting, would not be more loving. He would be morally asleep. The volume of Scripture that ties God to the cause of the poor and the abused is the same Scripture that promises he will judge.

The third, and deepest, is the cross. Whatever hell is, the Christian God is not a tyrant inflicting a fate he kept clear of. He stepped into the judgment himself. The astonishing center of the gospel is that God so refuses to send people to hell that he went there in their place, drinking the cup so that any who will may pass it by. That is not a God looking for reasons to condemn. It is a God who exhausted heaven to keep you out of it.

So the question hell finally presses is not how could a loving God. It is what will you do with a love that went that far and still will not force the door. The one who made you will not drag you into joy against your will. He will, with tears, let you have what you choose.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Faithful Christians hold different views on the nature and duration of final judgment, including eternal conscious torment, conditional immortality or annihilationism in which the lost finally cease to be, and a wider hope that God's mercy may reach further than we can see. Scripture is taken seriously by all three, and none should be declared the obvious reading.

questions.question: Is hell really eternal?
questions.shortAnswer: This is a genuine question within historic Christianity, not a settled one, and honest believers read the same passages and reach different conclusions. We will lay out the main positions fairly rather than pretend there is only one.
questions.answer:
Is hell really eternal is a question many thoughtful Christians ask with real anguish, not to dodge accountability but because the idea of unending conscious torment seems hard to square with a God of love. It is worth knowing that faithful believers who hold a high view of Scripture have landed in more than one place here, and the differences turn on how to read a handful of difficult words.

The traditional view, held by most of the church through most of its history, is that hell is conscious and everlasting, a final and irreversible state of separation from God. Its defenders point to the strong language of Jesus, who spoke of hell more than anyone, of eternal punishment set in parallel with eternal life, and they argue that the same word eternal cannot mean unending for the one and temporary for the other in the same sentence.

A second view, called conditional immortality or annihilationism, is held by some equally serious students of Scripture. They argue that the soul is not inherently immortal, that the Bible's language of destruction, perishing, and the second death should be taken seriously, and that the lost finally cease to exist rather than suffering forever. On this reading the punishment is eternal in its result, not in its ongoing duration. They would say this takes the warnings with full weight while resolving the moral strain.

A third stream has always hoped, more quietly, for a wider mercy, though the historic church has been cautious about pressing it into certainty, since Scripture's warnings are too sharp to explain away.

What all faithful views share is more important than where they differ. All agree that judgment is real, that what we do with Christ matters eternally, that no one is treated unjustly, and that hell, whatever its exact nature, is a horror to be warned of and not a topic for speculation or cruelty. C.S. Lewis's image holds across the views: the door of hell is locked from the inside, the tragedy of people finally getting the separation from God they insisted on. So hold the seriousness without pretending to more precision than Scripture gives, and let the whole sober subject do what Jesus meant it to do, drive us and the people we love toward the mercy that went to a cross to keep us out of it.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: This question is itself a place of genuine difference, between eternal conscious torment, conditional immortality or annihilationism, and a wider hope. The doctrine of last things is where the church has worked through these readings, and none should be presented as plainly obvious.

questions.question: What happens to us when we die?
questions.shortAnswer: The Christian hope is not mainly about a soul drifting off to a distant heaven. It is about resurrection, the promise that God will one day raise and restore the whole person, body included.
questions.answer:
Nobody comes back to file a report, so this is the question under all the others, and the honest place to start is with what the Bible does and does not say. It is more reserved than the paintings and the funeral poems, and more hopeful than either.

The Bible describes an intermediate state, a between. When a believer dies, the New Testament speaks of being away from the body and at home with the Lord, of being with Christ, which is better by far. Jesus told the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise. This is real and it is conscious and it is good, a being-with-Jesus that begins at once. But it is not the end of the story, and here most popular thinking stops too soon.

The Christian hope is not finally about going to heaven as a disembodied soul. It is resurrection. The between is a waiting room, not the destination. The destination is the day when Christ returns, the dead are raised with new bodies like his risen body, and heaven and earth are joined in a renewed creation. N.T. Wright calls the popular picture life after death, and the real biblical hope life after life after death, the bodily resurrection on the far side of the waiting. We were made to be embodied, and redemption does not cancel that. It completes it.

The Bible is also sober that not everyone is walking toward the same end. It speaks of a real judgment and a real possibility of being finally outside the life of God, which is why the question is not academic. Death is not a door everyone strolls through into the same garden. What you do with Christ matters, precisely because death is not the end of you.

For the grieving believer, the comfort is specific and strong. Your loved one who trusted Christ is not gone into nothing, nor drifting as a memory. They are with him now, and they will be raised. And the separation, the Bible dares to say, is temporary. That is not denial dressed as faith. It is the oldest Christian hope, that the last enemy to be destroyed is death itself.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on the intermediate state, with most holding that believers are consciously present with Christ between death and resurrection and some holding a view of soul sleep until the resurrection. All hold the bodily resurrection as the final hope.

questions.question: Why didn't God answer my prayer?
questions.shortAnswer: Sometimes the most faithful prayer, prayed by the most faithful person, still gets a no, and the Bible does not hide this from us. Jesus himself asked for a cup to pass and it did not.
questions.answer:
It helps to name how much this hurts before reaching for any reason. You asked for healing, for a marriage, for a child, for a life, and the answer did not come, or came as no. The faith does not tell you to feel fine about that. Paul asked three times for a thorn to be removed and it stayed. Jesus, in the garden, asked his Father to take the cup, and the cup came anyway.

So the New Testament's own heroes prayed prayers that were not granted as asked, which means an unanswered prayer is not proof that God is absent or that you prayed wrong. Sometimes the answer is no, and the reason is hidden from us in this life. Sometimes it is not yet. Sometimes, in ways we only see much later, the thing we begged for would have cost us more than we knew. And sometimes we simply do not get to know, and the faith does not pretend otherwise.

What it refuses is the cruel teaching that enough faith always gets the result. That teaching turns God into a machine and turns your grief into your failure. Jesus prayed with perfect faith and still drank the cup. Your unanswered prayer puts you beside him, not outside the family.

Keep praying anyway, even the angry prayers, even the ones that feel like talking to a closed door. The Bible is full of them, and they were heard.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how directly to expect God to intervene in response to prayer, with some emphasizing expectant prayer for healing and provision and others emphasizing trust in God's hidden purpose when prayers go unanswered. Both affirm that God hears and that faith does not guarantee the outcome we ask for.

questions.question: Can I actually trust the Bible?
questions.shortAnswer: Trusting the Bible is reasonable, not blind. The texts we have are remarkably well preserved, written close to the events they describe, and willing to record things no one inventing a religion would invent.
questions.answer:
Can you trust the Bible is really several questions wearing one coat. Has the text been preserved, or changed in transmission. Were the accounts written close enough to the events to count. And does the world they describe match what we can otherwise know. Each can be answered, and none requires checking your mind at the door.

On preservation, the New Testament is the best-attested document of the ancient world by an enormous margin. We have thousands of Greek manuscripts, some fragments within a century or two of the originals, against a handful of late copies for most classical works. The textual critic Bruce Metzger spent a career cataloguing the variants, and the honest result is this: the overwhelming majority are spelling and word order, the genuinely uncertain readings are footnoted in any decent Bible, and not one disputed reading puts a single doctrine of the faith in doubt. The story you are reading is the story they wrote.

On the sources, the Gospels were written within living memory of the events, while eyewitnesses were still alive to correct them, and the earliest creed Paul cites in 1 Corinthians 15 can be dated to within a few years of the crucifixion. The scholar Richard Bauckham has argued in detail that the Gospels read like eyewitness testimony, naming specific people who would have been known to the first readers. This is not the profile of legend, which needs generations to grow.

On the world they describe, archaeology has a long record of confirming the incidental details the Bible mentions in passing, the pool of Bethesda, Pilate, the politarchs of Thessalonica, names and titles once dismissed as errors and later dug out of the ground. None of this proves the miracles. It does show that the writers knew the places and times they claimed to know.

What trust does not mean is that every line is a flat literal report with no poetry, no genre, no human author with a style. The Bible contains law, song, proverb, history, letter, and apocalyptic vision, and reading it well means reading each as what it is. To trust it is not to ignore those differences. It is to believe that through them, God has spoken, reliably and on purpose. The honest question is not whether educated people can trust this book. Many of the people who know it best trust it most. The question is what you will do with it once you do.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians hold differing views on exactly how to describe the Bible as inspired, from strict inerrancy to a focus on its trustworthiness in all it teaches, while sharing the conviction that it is God's reliable word.

questions.question: Why are there four Gospels, and do they contradict each other?
questions.shortAnswer: There are four accounts because four witnesses tell one story from different angles, and the differences between them look like real testimony rather than a rehearsed script.
questions.answer:
Why are there four Gospels, and do they contradict each other is a fair question, and the honest answer is that the differences are real, they are exactly what you would expect, and they are a mark of genuine faith rather than a problem to hide.

Start with why four. The early church could have flattened them into one, and a man named Tatian actually tried, stitching them into a single harmony. The church declined and kept all four, because four witnesses to one Jesus are richer than one. Matthew writes to show Jesus as the promised Jewish Messiah, Mark as the suffering servant in a hurry, Luke as the savior of the outsider and the poor, John as the eternal Word made flesh. Same Jesus, four angles, like four portraits of one person rather than four photographs that must match pixel for pixel.

The differences are mostly differences of selection, arrangement, and emphasis, which every honest account makes. One writer mentions one angel at the tomb, another mentions two, the kind of variation you get from real witnesses describing the same scene, not the suspicious word-for-word agreement of people who colluded. Courts know this. When testimonies match too perfectly, you suspect a rehearsed story. When they agree on the core and differ in the details, you are likely hearing independent memory. The Gospels have exactly that texture.

And on the core, they do not waver. Jesus of Nazareth taught and healed, claimed a unique authority, was crucified under Pilate, and was found by his followers to be risen. The empty tomb, the cross, the identity, the resurrection, all four hold the line together. The apparent contradictions, examined, are nearly always differences of perspective or compression, the same event told from a different seat in the room.

So do not let the existence of four accounts, or the small variations among them, unsettle you. It would be far stranger, and far more suspicious, if four first-century writers from different places and audiences produced four identical texts. What we have instead looks like what real testimony looks like: united on what matters, varied in the way truthful witnesses always are.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how to harmonize particular details, such as the order of events or the exact wording of sayings, while agreeing the four accounts give one coherent witness to Jesus.

questions.question: Is the God of the Old Testament a different, angry God?
questions.shortAnswer: It is the same God across both Testaments, and the Old Testament shows that God to be patient and merciful far more often than wrathful. The contrast people feel is real, but it is not a change in character.
questions.answer:
Plenty of people, including some who grew up in church, carry a quiet theory that the Old Testament God is a wrathful tribal deity and the New Testament God, thanks to Jesus, finally mellowed. It is a very old idea. A man named Marcion taught it in the second century, wanted to cut the Old Testament out of the Bible entirely, and the church declared him a heretic for it. The reasons they did still hold.

The theory does not survive actually reading both Testaments. The Old Testament overflows with tenderness: the Lord is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, a phrase repeated like a refrain. He is the one who carries Israel like a father carries a child, who will not break a bruised reed. Meanwhile the New Testament is not all comfort. The most vivid descriptions of judgment in the whole Bible come from the lips of Jesus, and the book of Revelation is not a gentle read. The same God runs through both, holy and merciful from cover to cover.

What changes is not God's character but the stage of the story. The Old Testament shows God forming one nation in a violent ancient world, often meeting them where they were and leading them slowly toward something better, a long arc bending toward the day the rescue would come for everyone. The severity and the mercy are both there throughout, because real love is not the same as being permissive, and a God indifferent to evil, to the slave and the orphan and the crushed, would not be more loving but less.

The deepest answer is that Jesus did not come to correct the Old Testament God. He came as the Old Testament God in the flesh, the fullest picture of the very one who spoke from Sinai. He read those Scriptures as his Father's word, quoted them constantly, and said he came not to abolish them but to fulfill them. If Jesus is the clearest window into God's heart, and he treasured the Hebrew Scriptures, then the problem is not two Gods. It is that we have read the first Testament carelessly, and that we, like everyone, prefer a God with the judgment edited out until the day we need him to judge.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how to read the hardest passages of conquest and judgment, but they agree the God of both Testaments is one and unchanging in character.

questions.question: Hasn't science disproved the Bible?
questions.shortAnswer: Science and the Bible answer different kinds of questions, and many of the people who built modern science read the Bible as true. What science describes is how the world works, not whether it was made or why.
questions.answer:
Hasn't science disproved the Bible is a sentence that sounds like a settled verdict and is actually a category confusion, and clearing it up does not require pitting one against the other. Science and Scripture are mostly answering different questions, and the supposed war between them is more recent and more manufactured than people think.

Start with what each is for. Science asks how the physical world works, by what mechanism and on what timescale. The Bible asks who made it, why, and what it means, and what a human life is for. How and why are different questions, and answering one does not cancel the other. Knowing the chemistry of combustion does not tell you whether the candle was lit in love or in arson. Most of the famous conflicts evaporate once you notice the questions are not the same.

It is worth retiring the myth that faith and science have always been at war. The historians of science have largely dismantled that story. Modern science was born in a Christian civilization, often in the hands of devout believers, precisely because they expected an orderly creation made by a rational God to be intelligible and worth investigating. Kepler, Newton, Boyle, Faraday, Mendel the monk who founded genetics, Lemaitre the priest who first proposed the Big Bang. The lab was not enemy territory. For many it was an act of worship.

Where genuine tension shows up, it is usually over the interpretation of a few chapters, chiefly the opening of Genesis, and there, as elsewhere, the question is what kind of writing it is. Read as ancient theological literature making claims about the Creator and the creature, rather than as a science textbook, the supposed contradictions largely dissolve, and faithful Christians hold a range of views on the age of the earth and the mechanism of life without abandoning either the Bible or the data.

So science has not disproved the Bible, because science is not in the business of weighing the Bible's actual claims, that the universe was made on purpose, that it is good, that you bear the image of God, that Christ rose. Those are not the kind of statement a microscope can refute. Take the real findings of science seriously, take the actual claims of Scripture seriously, and the war you were promised turns out to be a quarrel between a bad reading of one and a tired myth about the other.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Faithful Christians hold young-earth, old-earth, and evolutionary-creation views of how God made the world, and most treat this as a third-order matter that does not divide the church.

questions.question: Do I have to choose between evolution and Genesis?
questions.shortAnswer: No. Genesis tells you that God made everything and made it good, and faithful Christians disagree about the mechanism and the timing without breaking fellowship over it.
questions.answer:
Many people believe they must choose: accept evolution and abandon the Bible, or keep the Bible and reject science. That framing is doing a great deal of damage, and it is not forced on you by the text or by the data.

The first question is not biology but interpretation. What is Genesis 1 trying to do. Read alongside the creation stories of the ancient Near East, it reads less like a lab report and more like a deliberate polemic. Where the neighbors had the world born from the corpse of a slain god and humans made as slaves, Genesis has one God speaking calmly, calling the world good, and crowning it with humans made in his own image. Its quarrel is with the gods of Babylon, not with the journals of biology. It tells you who made the world and why, and whose image you bear. It is largely silent on the mechanism and the stopwatch.

Once you see that, the options open up, and serious believers hold each. Young-earth creationists read the days literally. Old-earth creationists read them as ages or as a framework and accept the deep timescales. A large number, including the geneticist Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project and founded BioLogos, hold evolutionary creation: that evolution is the means God used, the patient process by which he filled the good world he intended. What unites these believers is the conviction that the universe is not an accident, that it was made on purpose, and that humans are not cosmic debris but image-bearers.

It helps to remember this is not a new compromise invented under pressure. Augustine, writing about Genesis in the fifth century, warned Christians against insisting on readings that contradict what can actually be known about the natural world, because it brings the faith into needless ridicule. B.B. Warfield, the great defender of biblical inerrancy a century ago, was open to evolution as God's method. The hard line is the recent novelty, not the careful reading.

What the Bible will not surrender is the theology: a real Creator, a creation that is good and not an illusion, humans uniquely made for God, and a real fall into sin. You can hold all of that without a position on the fossil record. So do not let anyone, believer or skeptic, force you to trade your mind for your faith. The God of Scripture is also the God of the world the scientists are studying, and truth does not finally divide against itself.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians hold young-earth, old-earth, and evolutionary-creation views, and treat the question of mechanism and age as a third-order matter rather than a dividing line.

questions.question: Did the miracles really happen?
questions.shortAnswer: If there is a God who made the world, then a miracle is not a broken law of nature but the maker acting freely within his own house. The real question is not whether miracles can happen, but whether this one, the resurrection, did.
questions.answer:
Did the miracles really happen, or are they later legends the church added to a simple teacher. This is a reasonable suspicion, and how you answer it depends less on the historical evidence than on a prior question most people never examine: whether miracles are possible at all.

The philosopher David Hume framed the modern objection, that miracles violate the laws of nature and the testimony for them can never outweigh our uniform experience that nature runs on rails. But notice the hidden move. If you assume in advance that a God who acts cannot exist, then no amount of evidence for a miracle will ever be enough, because you have ruled it out before looking. That is not a conclusion from the evidence. It is a filter placed over the evidence. The question of miracles is downstream of the question of God. If there is a God who made the laws of nature, then his acting within them is no more a violation than a composer changing his own theme.

Set the filter aside and the historical picture is not what the legend theory predicts. The accounts are early, within the lifetime of eyewitnesses, far too soon for legend to have replaced living memory. The miracles are woven into the fabric of the story rather than tacked on as decoration. Even hostile ancient sources did not deny that Jesus did astonishing things; they attributed his power to dark forces rather than claiming nothing happened, which is its own kind of admission. And the central miracle, the resurrection, is not a quiet add-on but the load-bearing claim the whole movement was built on and died for.

C.S. Lewis, who once held the skeptical view, argued that the Christian miracles are not random magic but signs, small previews of what the Maker is doing on a large scale, water to wine because he makes wine every year through the vine, multiplied bread because he multiplies grain in every field, the dead raised because he is the one who made life to begin with. They fit the character of the one performing them.

None of this forces belief, and it is not meant to. It is meant to remove the lazy assumption that intelligent people simply know miracles do not happen. They do not know that. They have assumed it. The real question is not whether the reports are too good to be true, but whether there is a God of the kind who would, and could, do such things, and that question the resurrection puts squarely on the table.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians agree the resurrection is real and central, while differing on how to read certain other miracle accounts and how God works through ordinary means today.

questions.question: Where do I even start reading the Bible?
questions.shortAnswer: Start with a Gospel, not at page one. Read Mark or John first to meet Jesus, then Genesis for the beginning of the story, then Psalms for prayer and Romans for the heart of the message.
questions.answer:
Most people open to Genesis, push through to the middle of the law, and quietly give up. There is a better way in. Begin with one of the four Gospels, because the whole book is finally about the person they describe. Mark is short and fast and good if you want the bones of it. John is slower and deeper and good if you want to sit with who Jesus claims to be.

Once you have met him, go back to Genesis to see where the story starts, how the world was made and how it broke. Then let the Psalms teach you how to pray, since they give honest words for joy, anger, grief, and trust without pretending. After that, read Romans slowly, because it lays out the core of the message more directly than anywhere else.

Read a little at a time and ask one question of each passage. What does this show me about God, and what does it ask of me. If a reference or a piece of background trips you up, use the Passage Context Tool on this site to see where a verse sits in the larger story before you draw a conclusion from it. The goal is not to finish fast. It is to be changed.

questions.question: Was Jesus really God, or just a good teacher?
questions.shortAnswer: The 'good teacher' option is the one the evidence does not allow, because Jesus claimed an identity no merely good teacher would claim. Christians believe he was telling the truth.
questions.answer:
There is a popular middle position that Jesus was a great moral teacher, a wise man, but not divine. It sounds humble and generous. C.S. Lewis pointed out that it is the one option Jesus himself does not leave open. A merely great teacher does not forgive sins committed against other people, accept worship, claim to existed before Abraham, and say that he and the Father are one. A man who said those things while being only a man would be either a liar, or a lunatic on the level of someone claiming to be a poached egg, or else he was telling the truth. The polite third category, good teacher, is not on the menu.

The claims are scattered all through the earliest material, not invented centuries later. He receives worship and does not stop it, which a faithful Jew would have found blasphemous. He applies to himself the divine name from Exodus, I am. He forgives sins, and his critics rightly note that only God can do that. The scholar Richard Bauckham has shown that the first Christians, who were monotheistic Jews, did the unthinkable almost immediately: they included Jesus inside the identity of the one God of Israel, worshiping him without believing they had abandoned their monotheism.

The formal language came later, but it was defending what was already there, not inventing something new. At the Council of Nicaea in 325 the church confessed the Son to be of one substance with the Father against the teaching of Arius, who held that there was a time when the Son was not. At Chalcedon in 451 it confessed Jesus to be fully God and fully man, two natures in one person, without confusion and without division. These councils were guardrails around a mystery the church had been living inside from the start.

Why does it matter whether he was only a teacher or actually God? Because if he was only a teacher, he left advice, and we have plenty of advice. If he was God in the flesh, then in him the maker of the universe has a human face, and his death is not a tragedy but a rescue, and his words are not suggestions but the voice of the one who made you. Everything hangs on it. The question is not whether Jesus was nice. It is whether he was who he said he was.

questions.question: How do we know Jesus actually rose from the dead?
questions.shortAnswer: No one can hand you a video, but the historical case rests on facts most scholars grant and asks which explanation accounts for all of them. The empty tomb and the changed witnesses are hard to dismiss.
questions.answer:
Christianity is unusual among religions in that it stakes everything on a historical claim that could, in principle, be falsified. Paul says it without hedging: if Christ has not been raised, our faith is worthless and we are to be pitied. So the resurrection is not a symbol the faith could survive without. It is the load-bearing wall.

Historians who study the period, believing and skeptical alike, tend to agree on a short list of facts that any theory has to explain. Jesus was executed by crucifixion and buried. His tomb was found empty. His followers, and at least two skeptics, James his brother and Paul his persecutor, had experiences they were certain were encounters with him alive. And the movement exploded in the very city where his body could have been produced to end it, and never was. Gary Habermas built much of his work around this minimal-facts approach, granting only what the broad scholarly consensus grants.

The alternative explanations are old and each one strains. The disciples lied: but people do not endure torture and death for what they know to be a hoax, and nearly all of them did. They hallucinated: but groups do not share the same detailed hallucination over weeks, and hallucinations do not leave an empty tomb. The authorities moved the body: then producing it would have strangled the church in its crib. Notice too that the first witnesses named are women, whose testimony carried little legal weight in that world. No one inventing a story for first-century readers would build it on witnesses no one was expected to believe. That detail smells like memory, not marketing.

The historian N.T. Wright, in a nearly eight-hundred-page study, argues that neither pagan nor Jewish expectation can account for what the first Christians claimed. Jews believed in a resurrection at the end of the world, of everyone at once. Nobody expected one man to rise in the middle of history. Something happened that forced them to revise a belief they had held for centuries.

None of this compels faith, and it is not meant to. It is meant to clear the ground of the idea that only the gullible could believe it. The question the empty tomb leaves you with is not whether intelligent people can hold this. They can and do. The question is what you will do if it is true.

questions.question: How can God be three and one at the same time?
questions.shortAnswer: Christians do not claim God is three of the same thing and one of the same thing, which would be a contradiction. We claim one God in three persons, which is a mystery the church confesses without pretending to exhaust it.
questions.answer:
The Trinity is the doctrine everyone assumes is the most abstract and impractical, and it is actually the most important thing Christianity says about who God is. The claim is precise: there is one God, who exists eternally as three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet not three Gods. It is not a riddle invented to confuse you. It is the church refusing to let go of things the Bible would not let it let go of.

Two guardrails define it. The first is against tritheism, the idea of three Gods, which the Bible's relentless monotheism forbids: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The second is against modalism, the idea that God is one person wearing three masks at different times, which fails because the Father, Son, and Spirit speak to one another and love one another in the same scenes. At the baptism of Jesus, the Son stands in the water, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks from heaven. That is one moment, three persons.

The formal vocabulary was hammered out under pressure. At Nicaea in 325 the church rejected Arius and confessed the Son as of one substance with the Father. The Cappadocian fathers in the fourth century gave the language of one essence in three persons. Augustine, in his great work on the Trinity, warned that every analogy breaks: the water-ice-steam picture drifts toward modalism, the three-leaf clover toward tritheism. The Greek tradition spoke of perichoresis, the eternal mutual indwelling, the persons making room for one another in a kind of eternal dance.

Here is why it is not abstract at all. If God were a single solitary person, then before he made the world he was alone, and love would be something he learned by creating, something he needed us for. But if God is eternally three persons giving themselves to one another, then love is not something God does. It is what God is, before the universe existed, with no need of us at all. When the Bible says God is love, the Trinity is what makes that sentence true rather than sentimental. You were made by a community of self-giving love, and made for it.

questions.question: Why did Jesus have to die?
questions.shortAnswer: Because sin is a real debt against a real God, and Jesus chose to pay it himself rather than leave us to. The cross is where God's justice and God's mercy meet instead of cancel each other.
questions.answer:
Why did Jesus have to die is really two questions. Why did they kill him, and why did God will it. The first is history. The second is the heart of the gospel.

The historical answer is plain enough. Jesus threatened the religious establishment by claiming an authority that belonged to God alone, and he threatened Rome by being hailed as a king. A coalition of frightened power did what frightened power does. But the New Testament insists the cross was not merely a miscarriage of justice that God reacted to. It was, somehow, the plan, foreshadowed for centuries, the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world.

So why would God will it. The Bible piles up images rather than a single equation, and the wisest theologians have held several together. The oldest is substitution: we owed a debt we could not pay, and Jesus paid it in our place, the just for the unjust, taking the judgment our sin had earned so that we would not have to. Anselm, in the eleventh century, framed it in terms of a debt to God's honor; the Reformers in terms of the law's penalty borne by a willing substitute. Alongside that runs the image of victory, what the old church called Christus Victor, the cross as the battlefield where Christ defeated sin, death, and the powers, looking like defeat and being the decisive win. And there is the image of love's demonstration, God proving once and for all the lengths to which he would go, dying for his enemies while they were still his enemies.

These are not rival theories so much as facets of one jewel. Strip out substitution and the cross becomes a moving gesture that accomplishes nothing real. Strip out love and it becomes a cold transaction. Hold them together and you get the scandal at the center of the faith: the Judge stepped down from the bench and took the sentence himself.

This is why Christians cannot treat the cross as a sad preliminary to Easter. It is the place where the holiness of God and the love of God meet without either being compromised. Justice is satisfied and mercy is poured out in the same act. That is what had to happen, and it is what did.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians describe how the cross works in more than one way, from substitution to victory over evil to a demonstration of love, and most hold these together rather than choosing only one.

questions.question: Is Jesus really the only way to God?
questions.shortAnswer: Christians hold that Jesus is the one savior of the world, not because Christianity is one club among many, but because of who they believe Jesus is. If he is God come to rescue us, then he is not one road among several.
questions.answer:
This is the claim the modern world finds most offensive: Jesus saying I am the way, the truth, and the life, no one comes to the Father except through me. It sounds arrogant, even dangerous, in a society that prizes tolerance above almost everything. The objection deserves a real answer, not a softening.

Start by noticing that the popular alternative is not as humble as it looks. The famous picture is several blind men touching different parts of an elephant, each grasping only a piece, none seeing the whole. It is meant to teach humility. But to tell the story you have to be the one person in the room who can see the whole elephant and knows the blind men are mistaken. The pluralist who says all religions are partial glimpses of the same truth has quietly claimed the very thing he denies to everyone else, a view from above. Lesslie Newbigin, who spent decades as a missionary in India among genuinely devout people of other faiths, saw this clearly. There is no neutral ground. Everyone is standing somewhere.

It also helps to see that the religions are not in fact saying the same thing. They make contradictory claims about the most basic questions, whether God is personal, whether the self is real, what is wrong with us, and what the rescue is. They cannot all be true at once any more than contradictory maps can all lead home. Respecting them means taking their differences seriously, not flattening them into a vague sameness none of their adherents would recognize.

What makes the Christian claim bearable, even good, is its content. Christianity does not say we are the way because our group is superior or our morality is better. It says no one climbs to God, that all our climbing falls short, and that God came down. The exclusivity is not a velvet rope around a club. It is a rescue in a single lifeboat. Tim Keller noted that a truly narrow, self-righteous religion produces proud people, while the message of a God crucified for his enemies, if you actually believe it, produces the humblest people on earth, because it tells you that you are saved by sheer mercy and not by being right.

And the door is wider than the offense suggests. The one way is not a wall to keep people out. It is a person with his arms open, and the invitation in the last page of the Bible is simple: let the one who is thirsty come.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Faithful Christians agree Christ is the one savior but differ on the fate of those who never hear of him, a question taken up in the next entry.

questions.question: What about people who never heard of Jesus?
questions.shortAnswer: This is one of the most pressing questions a thoughtful person can ask, and Scripture does not give a tidy formula. What it does promise is that the Judge of all the earth will do right.
questions.answer:
What about the person who lived and died having never heard of Jesus, through no fault of their own. This is not a debating trick. It is one of the most pressing moral questions the faith faces, and the honest answer begins with humility about how much we are told.

Start with what is clear. The Bible says God is perfectly just and also genuinely good, that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and that he is the judge of all the earth who will do right. Whatever happens to the unevangelized, it will not be unfair. The Judge can be trusted even where the verdict is hidden from us. That alone answers the emotional force of the question, even before the theology.

Scripture also says that no one is a blank slate. Paul argues that creation itself testifies to a Creator, and that conscience writes a moral law on every heart, so that people are responsible for what they do with the light they have, however dim. No one is judged for rejecting a name they never heard. People are judged for what they did with what they were given.

From there, faithful Christians divide, and it is worth knowing the range. The restrictivist view holds that explicit faith in Christ is necessary, which makes the missionary task urgent. The inclusivist view, held by figures as orthodox as C.S. Lewis, holds that Christ is still the only Savior, but that God may apply that salvation to some who responded to the light they had without knowing his name, the way Old Testament believers were saved by a Christ they could not yet see. There is also a strong biblical theme that God moves heaven and earth to get the gospel to those who are seeking, sending a Philip to the one Ethiopian on the road.

What all faithful positions refuse is the cynicism that says it does not matter, and the arrogance that says we have God's filing system memorized. Salvation is through Christ alone. How widely God applies that, in cases we cannot see, we leave to a Judge who loved the world enough to die for it. And we let the weight of the question do what it is meant to do: send us to tell people, rather than to speculate about them.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Some hold explicit faith in Christ is necessary for salvation, others that God may justly save some who never heard through Christ's work on the basis of the light they were given, with various positions in between, while all agree salvation comes only through Christ.

questions.question: Aren't all religions basically saying the same thing?
questions.shortAnswer: They share real moral wisdom, and that common ground is worth honoring. But on the questions that matter most, who God is and how we are made right with him, they say genuinely different things.
questions.answer:
It is true that the great faiths often agree about kindness, honesty, generosity, and the dignity of human life. That overlap is not nothing. A person who treats those agreements as a sign of shared conscience is seeing something true. We should not flatten other believers into caricatures or pretend they teach nothing good.

But to say all religions are the same is, in its own way, disrespectful to each of them. It tells the Muslim, the Hindu, the Buddhist, and the Jew that the very thing they hold most precious does not really matter. They would not recognize themselves in the claim that the differences are cosmetic.

The differences are real and they are deep. Is God personal or impersonal. Is the human problem ignorance, or imbalance, or guilt before a holy God. Is salvation something we achieve or something we receive. These are not the same answer in different clothes. They are different answers, and they cannot all be true at once.

Respecting another faith means taking its actual claims seriously enough to disagree where you must. The Christian claim is specific. God came to us in Jesus and did for us what we could not do for ourselves. That is either true or it is not, and it is worth examining on its own terms rather than dissolving into a vague sameness no one actually believes.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians agree the faiths genuinely differ on God and salvation, while differing among themselves over how much truth God has made available within other religious traditions.

questions.question: What is grace, really?
questions.shortAnswer: Grace is God giving you what you have not earned and could never earn. Not a reward for the good. A gift for the undeserving, which is everyone.
questions.answer:
We use the word grace for graceful dancers and gracious hosts, and we lose what it meant. Grace is favor you did not earn and cannot pay back. It runs against every instinct we have, because we are built to keep score.

Religion, at its worst, is a ladder. Do more, sin less, climb higher, and maybe God will be pleased. Grace cuts the ladder down. It says the climbing was never going to work, and God came down to you instead. You are accepted first, and the obedience grows out of the acceptance, not the other way around.

This is why grace offends respectable people more than it offends sinners. The sinner knows he needs a gift. The respectable man wants a wage. But God does not pay wages for righteousness, because none of us has earned one.

You are loved at your worst. That is not permission to stay there. It is the only thing strong enough to change you.

questions.question: If I am forgiven, why do I still sin?
questions.shortAnswer: Because forgiveness and full healing are not the same moment. You are pardoned now, and you are being remade slowly. The war you feel is evidence you are alive, not proof you are fake.
questions.answer:
Many Christians carry a quiet panic. They were told that meeting Jesus would fix them, and then they kept failing, and they wondered if it ever took. It took. You are just feeling something the New Testament describes plainly.

The Bible draws a line between justification, being declared right with God in an instant, and sanctification, being made actually holy over a lifetime. The first is finished. The second is in progress. You are pardoned fully and healed gradually, and the gap between those two is where the struggle lives.

Paul, near the end of his life, still wrote about doing the thing he hated. That was not a young convert. That was an apostle. The presence of the fight is not the absence of grace. A dead man does not struggle against sin. The struggle itself is a sign the Spirit is in you.

So do not measure your standing by your feelings on a bad day. Measure it by the cross. Then get up and keep walking. Slow growth is still growth.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on how much victory over sin to expect in this life. Some traditions emphasize ongoing struggle until death, others a deeper work of the Spirit that breaks sin's grip more decisively. All agree perfection waits for the resurrection.

questions.question: Is it okay to be angry at God?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes. The Bible is full of people who told God exactly how they felt. He can hold your anger. What he asks is that you bring it to him instead of walking away.
questions.answer:
Somewhere we picked up the idea that good faith is calm faith, that real believers do not get angry with God. The Bible never says this. A third of the Psalms are complaints, and some of them are furious.

Job accused God to his face. Jeremiah said God had deceived him. The Psalmist asked how long, over and over, with no answer in sight. None of them were struck down for it. The honesty was counted as faith, because they were still talking to God, not about him from a distance.

There is a difference between anger that turns toward God and anger that turns away. The first is prayer, even when it shakes. The second is the slow drift into a closed heart. God can take the shouting. What grieves him is the silence of a person who has decided he is not worth the conversation.

So say it. Tell him where it hurts and why you are angry. The door he wants open is the one you slam when you go quiet.

questions.question: What is heaven actually like?
questions.shortAnswer: Less like clouds and harps than you were told. The Christian hope is not floating spirits but a renewed creation, resurrected bodies, and God dwelling with his people on a healed earth.
questions.answer:
Ask most people to picture heaven and they imagine disembodied souls on clouds, which sounds boring because it would be. That picture owes more to cartoons than to Scripture.

The Bible's hope is louder and more physical than that. It ends not with us escaping to heaven but with heaven coming down, a new heaven and a new earth, the city of God on a renewed creation. The dead are not left as ghosts. They are raised, given bodies like the risen Jesus, who ate fish after he rose.

What makes it heaven is not the architecture. It is the presence. The promise is that God will dwell with his people, wipe every tear, and end death itself. Everything that breaks here will be mended there, and the mending will be permanent.

So the Christian does not hope to leave the world behind forever. He hopes for the world made right, with the curtain between God and us finally torn down for good.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on the details and timing of the end, and on how literally to read the imagery in Revelation. The core they share is bodily resurrection, a renewed creation, and unbroken life with God.

questions.question: Why did God command the killing of the Canaanites?
questions.shortAnswer: It is one of the hardest passages in the Bible, and it should not be smoothed over. There are honest things to say about judgment, the language of the ancient world, and Jesus, but no answer that makes it comfortable.
questions.answer:
This is the question that makes thoughtful readers close the Bible, and pretending it is easy does more harm than the question does. So start by admitting it is terrible to read.

A few things belong in the room. The conquest is framed as judgment on generations of entrenched evil, including child sacrifice, not as ethnic hatred. The language of total destruction was a known ancient way of describing decisive defeat, and the same books that say all were destroyed go on to describe survivors, which suggests the rhetoric was not a literal body count. And this was a specific, bounded command tied to one moment in redemptive history, never a standing pattern for God's people.

None of that dissolves the horror, and it should not. What it does is locate it. The deepest Christian answer is not a clever defense but a person. The God who is revealed fully in Jesus weeps at tombs, dies for his enemies, and tells his followers to put the sword away. Whatever we make of Joshua, we read it back through Calvary, not the other way around.

Hold the tension honestly. A faith that can only survive by hiding its hardest pages is not worth much. This one does not ask you to hide them.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ widely here: some read the conquest accounts as largely hyperbolic ancient war language, some emphasize divine judgment on specific evil, some wrestle with it as a genuine moral difficulty held in tension with the character of Christ. Faithful readers land in different places.

questions.question: Why are there so many Bible translations, and which one is right?
questions.shortAnswer: Because translating ancient languages forces real choices between word-for-word precision and natural readability. The differences are mostly about style, not message. Pick a trustworthy one you will actually read.
questions.answer:
Walk into a bookstore and the wall of Bibles can feel like a reason to doubt. If the experts cannot agree on the words, how can any of it be trusted? But the variety is a sign of care, not confusion.

Every translation sits somewhere on a line. On one end is word-for-word, which keeps the original structure but can read stiffly. On the other is thought-for-thought, which reads smoothly but makes more interpretive calls for you. A paraphrase goes further still, restating ideas in fresh language. None of these is dishonest. They are answering the same question differently: how do you carry meaning across a few thousand years and a very different language.

What matters is that the core is stable across all of them. No doctrine of the faith rises or falls on which mainstream translation you hold. The places that differ are mostly matters of phrasing, and good Bibles footnote the genuinely uncertain spots openly.

So do not let the wall paralyze you. Choose a respected translation in language you understand, and then do the one thing all the arguing can distract you from. Read it.
