If you can rest in that, you can afford to be charitable about the thousand years. The kingdom does not depend on us getting the chart right. It depends on the King, and He is not in doubt.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The three historic positions are premillennialism (Christ returns before a literal earthly thousand-year reign), amillennialism (the millennium is the present reign of Christ between His comings, with His return bringing the final judgment and new creation), and postmillennialism (Christ returns after a gospel-driven golden age). Premillennialism appears in early fathers like Irenaeus and Justin Martyr and dominates much modern evangelicalism, especially in its dispensational form. Amillennialism, shaped by Augustine, has been the majority view in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and much Reformed thought. Postmillennialism flourished among Puritans and nineteenth-century Protestants. None is excluded by the ecumenical creeds, and all affirm Christ's reign, His return, final judgment, and the new creation.

questions.question: Who or what is the antichrist?
questions.category: Last things and the return of Christ
questions.shortAnswer: The antichrist is the great opponent of Christ at the end of the age, described as a deceiver who exalts himself against God. Scripture also says many antichrists are already at work, so the term names both a coming figure and a spirit of opposition present in every era.
questions.answer:
The word antichrist appears far less in the Bible than the cultural noise around it would suggest, and only in the letters of John. There he writes that his readers have heard the antichrist is coming, and that even now many antichrists have come, which is how they know it is the last hour (1 John 2:18). For John, an antichrist is anyone who denies that Jesus is the Christ, who denies the Father and the Son, who refuses to confess Jesus come in the flesh (1 John 2:22, 4:3). So the first thing Scripture does with the term is widen it. The antichrist is not only a single future villain. It is a spirit of denial already loose in the world, and it works through false teaching, not just political power.

Alongside this, the New Testament does point to a climactic figure. Paul warns the Thessalonians of the man of lawlessness, the son of destruction, who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god, taking his seat in the temple of God and proclaiming himself to be God (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4). Paul says this figure is currently restrained and will be revealed at the proper time, and that the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of His mouth at His coming. This is a real and disturbing prophecy of a final, concentrated rebellion, an idolatry of self that reaches its peak just before Christ returns to end it.

The book of Revelation adds the imagery most people associate with the antichrist, though it never uses the word. There are two beasts, one from the sea and one from the earth, and the famous number 666, the number of the beast and of a man (Revelation 13:18). In its first-century setting, this language pointed unmistakably at the Roman Empire and its cult of emperor worship, which demanded that Caesar be honored as lord and god. The beast is tyranny that claims the worship owed to God alone. Many scholars note that the number 666, by the ancient practice of assigning numbers to letters, fits the name Nero Caesar, the emperor who persecuted Christians. So Revelation's beast had a concrete, present referent even as it pictures a recurring and final pattern.

This is why I think the wisest approach holds three things together. There is a spirit of antichrist, present in every age, wherever Christ is denied and human power claims divine honors. There have been many antichrist figures across history, tyrants and false teachers who embody that spirit, and the church has variously and often recklessly identified them, including Reformers who called the papacy antichrist and others who pinned the label on Nero, Hitler, Stalin, and a long line of contemporary figures who all turned out not to end the world. And there appears to be a final antichrist, a last and fullest embodiment of the rebellion, revealed just before the end. These are not competing readings so much as layers of the same reality.

What strikes me most, pastorally, is what John does with the doctrine. He does not use it to fuel speculation or fear. He uses it to test confession and to steady believers. The mark of antichrist is not a barcode or a political party. It is the denial of Jesus as the Christ come in the flesh. That means the most important antichrist detector is not watching the news but examining what a teacher says about Jesus. The deception John warns about is doctrinal before it is political, and it often comes from inside the religious community, dressed in the language of faith.

So resist two errors. Do not obsess, building elaborate identifications of the antichrist with whichever leader you fear, a game the church has played and lost for two thousand years. And do not dismiss, pretending there is no real and personal evil arrayed against Christ. The sober truth is in between. The spirit of antichrist is real and present, a final reckoning is coming, and Christ has already guaranteed the outcome. Paul does not tell the Thessalonians to be afraid of the man of lawlessness. He tells them how the story ends, with the Lord overthrowing him by the brightness of His coming. The antichrist, whoever and whenever, loses.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on whether the antichrist is primarily a single future individual, a succession of figures, a system or institution, or chiefly a spirit of opposition. Dispensational premillennialists typically expect a specific end-times world ruler who makes a covenant and is revealed during the tribulation. Many Reformers, including Luther and the Westminster Confession in its original form, identified the papacy as antichrist, a view few hold today. Preterists tie the beast and the man of lawlessness largely to Nero and first-century Rome. Amillennialists often see the antichrist as a recurring pattern of opposition culminating in a final figure. Catholic and Orthodox traditions generally expect a personal antichrist near the end while reading John's many antichrists as present heresy. All agree Christ defeats him decisively.

questions.question: Is the world really going to end? And should that scare me?
questions.category: Last things and the return of Christ
questions.shortAnswer: The present order of things will come to a decisive end when Christ returns, but the Bible's hope is not annihilation. It is renewal, the world remade rather than erased. For those in Christ, the end is not something to dread but something to long for.
questions.answer:
Yes, the Bible teaches that the world as we know it is heading toward an end. This is not a fearful add-on but part of the basic Christian view of history. Time is not an endless circle, the same seasons turning forever. It is a line with a beginning, when God created, and a destination, when God will bring all things to their appointed conclusion. Peter writes that the day of the Lord will come, and that the heavens will pass away and the elements will be dissolved (2 Peter 3:10). Jesus said heaven and earth will pass away, though His words will not (Matthew 24:35). So the honest answer is that this present order is not permanent.

But we have to be careful what we mean by end, because the popular imagination jumps straight to destruction, a planet incinerated, everything lost. The Bible's picture is stranger and far better. The same Peter who speaks of the heavens passing away goes on to say that we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Paul says creation itself waits with eager longing to be set free from its bondage to decay (Romans 8:21). The word often used is not destruction but renewal. What ends is the world's bondage to sin, death, and corruption. What remains, transfigured, is the world itself.

The best analogy is the resurrection of Jesus, which is the template for everything God intends to do with creation. His body in the tomb was not annihilated and replaced with a brand new one. It was the same body, raised, transformed, glorified, recognizable yet changed, no longer subject to death. So it will be with the cosmos. The end of the world is less like a building being demolished and more like a body being raised. There is real death involved, a genuine passing away, and then there is real continuity on the far side of it. The world dies and rises.

Should this scare you. The Bible's answer depends entirely on whose you are. For those who have built their whole existence on the present order, who have no hope beyond it and no peace with the God who made it, the end is rightly sobering. The same passages that promise renewal also promise judgment, a real accounting before a holy God (Revelation 20:11-15). I will not soften that, because softening it would be a kind of lying. But for those who belong to Christ, the tone of the New Testament is not terror. It is longing. The early Christians prayed for the end to come, because the end is when their Lord appears and their tears are wiped away.

This reframes how a Christian holds anxiety about the world. We are surrounded by end-of-the-world fears, ecological, nuclear, technological, and these fears are not foolish. Real catastrophes are possible, and we should work against them, because loving our neighbor includes the world our neighbor lives in. But the Christian is not finally at the mercy of these fears, because our hope was never that humanity would manage to keep the planet running forever by its own competence. Our hope is that the God who made it will redeem it. That frees us to work hard and to rest deep at the same time.

So I would say this to a frightened heart. Yes, this world will end, but ending is not the worst thing, and for the people of God it is not even a sad thing. The last word in the Bible is not a mushroom cloud. It is a city coming down out of heaven, a wedding, a God who dwells with His people and wipes every tear from their eyes, and a voice from the throne saying He is making all things new (Revelation 21:1-5). The end you are afraid of is not the end the Bible promises. The real end is a beginning that does not stop.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians agree the present order ends at Christ's return but differ on the nature of that end. Some emphasize a more literal destruction of the present cosmos followed by a fresh creation, reading 2 Peter 3 as the elements being burned up. Others, increasingly common in recent theology, emphasize continuity and renewal, reading the same passages as purifying judgment that transforms rather than annihilates, with the resurrection of Jesus as the model. There are also differences over timing tied to the millennial views, and over how literally to read apocalyptic imagery. Across these views, Christians share the conviction that history is heading toward Christ's return, a real judgment, and the new creation, not toward meaningless oblivion.

questions.question: What is the new heaven and new earth? Is heaven really our final home?
questions.category: Last things and the return of Christ
questions.shortAnswer: The new heaven and new earth is the renewed creation where God dwells with His people forever, the true and final home of the redeemed. Our ultimate hope is not to escape to heaven but for heaven and earth to be joined and made new.
questions.answer:
Most Christians, if asked where they will end up, would say heaven, picturing a place far off and elsewhere, immaterial, where saved souls float free of bodies and the earth is left behind. It is worth saying clearly that this is not quite the Bible's final picture. The New Testament's ultimate hope is not a one-way trip away from creation. It is the renewal of creation and the descent of God's presence into it. John writes that he saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, and a loud voice said that the dwelling place of God is now with man (Revelation 21:2-3). Notice the direction. The city comes down. God comes to dwell with us, here, in a remade world.

This fulfills a thread that runs from the very beginning. The Bible opens with God walking with humanity in a garden, heaven and earth overlapping, no separation between God's space and ours. Sin tore that apart and drove humanity out. The whole story since is God working to bring His presence back to His people. The tabernacle and temple were partial, localized returns of that presence. The incarnation, God dwelling among us in Christ, was the decisive one. And the new creation is the consummation, the moment heaven and earth are finally and fully reunited, and the prayer Jesus taught us, that God's will be done on earth as it is in heaven, is answered completely.

The scholar N. T. Wright has spent much of his career recovering this point for a church that had drifted into a vague heaven-as-escape spirituality, and he argues persuasively that the biblical hope is resurrection life in a renewed physical creation, not disembodied existence in a cloudy elsewhere. This matters enormously. It means the resurrection of the body is not a strange appendix to the faith but its very heart. We will not be ghosts. We will be raised, embodied, like the risen Christ, to live embodied lives in a real and renewed world. Isaiah pictured it as building houses and planting vineyards and enjoying the work of our hands, no longer in vain (Isaiah 65:21-23).

What will it be like. Scripture is restrained, and we should be too, but it gives us the shape. There will be no more death, no mourning, no crying, no pain, for the former things will have passed away (Revelation 21:4). There will be no temple in the city, because God Himself and the Lamb are its temple, the very thing every temple ever pointed toward (Revelation 21:22). There will be no sun, because the glory of God will be its light. And there will be the nations and their kings bringing their glory into it, which many take to mean that the redeemed cultures and achievements of human history, purified, are carried into the new world rather than discarded. Nothing good is finally wasted.

What does this do to how we live now. C. S. Lewis argued that the Christians who did most for the present world were precisely those who thought most of the next, and that aiming at heaven, you get earth thrown in, while aiming at earth you get neither. A solid hope in the new creation is not escapism. It is the opposite. If matter matters, if bodies will be raised and the earth renewed, then what we do with our bodies and our world now is not throwaway. Our labor in the Lord is not in vain, because it is somehow taken up into the world that lasts. The new creation dignifies the present one even as it relativizes it.

So is heaven our final home. In a sense, yes, but only because heaven is coming here. The believer who dies goes to be with Christ, which Paul calls far better, and that intermediate state is real comfort. But it is not the end of the story. The end of the story is resurrection and a renewed creation, God dwelling with His people in a world made whole, every tear wiped away by His own hand. We do not finally go up to God. He comes down to us, and stays. That is the home we were made for, and it is the home that is coming.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: There is broad agreement across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions on the core hope of resurrection and the new creation, all confessed in the creeds. Differences arise over emphasis and detail. Some traditions and popular piety stress the intermediate state and a more spiritual heaven, while recent biblical scholarship (notably N. T. Wright) has pressed the church to recover the bodily resurrection and renewed earth as the final hope. Catholics and Orthodox include purgation or purification of the soul before final glory, which most Protestants reject. There are differences over how literally to read Revelation's imagery and over the degree of continuity between this creation and the next. The shared conviction is that God will dwell forever with a redeemed, resurrected people in a renewed creation.

questions.question: What is the final judgment, and how should I think about being judged by God?
questions.category: Last things and the return of Christ
questions.shortAnswer: The final judgment is the day when the risen Christ judges every person who has ever lived, exposing all things and setting everything right. For those in Christ it is not a threat but a vindication, because the verdict has already been settled at the cross.
questions.answer:
Every culture has some instinct that wrongs must be answered, that the murderer who dies comfortably in old age has not actually gotten away with it, that the abused child crying in the dark deserves more than a shrug from the universe. The doctrine of final judgment takes that instinct and says it is true. History will not simply trail off into forgetfulness. There is a day appointed when God will judge the world in righteousness through the man He has appointed, and He has given assurance of this by raising Him from the dead (Acts 17:31). The Judge is Jesus, and His own resurrection is the down payment that the day is coming.

We have to feel the weight of it before we feel the comfort. Paul says we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10). John sees the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books are opened, and each is judged according to what he has done (Revelation 20:12). This is not a vague accounting. It is a real exposure of real lives, including the parts we have hidden from everyone, including ourselves. Jesus said that on the day of judgment people will give account even for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). Nothing is overlooked. That should sober anyone, and it sobers me when I let it.

But here is where the gospel changes the entire character of the day for the believer. The astonishing claim of the New Testament is that the verdict has already been announced in advance. The judgment that belongs to the last day has been brought forward to the cross, where Christ bore the condemnation His people deserved, so that there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The Judge is the one who was judged in our place. This means the Christian does not approach the judgment seat hoping the scales tip in their favor. They approach it clothed in a righteousness that is not their own, with the verdict already spoken over them in the resurrection of their Substitute.

This is why the New Testament can speak of believers facing the judgment with confidence rather than terror. John writes that love has been perfected among us so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as He is, so also are we in this world, and perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:17-18). Read that slowly. The Christian's confidence on the last day is not arrogance and not denial of sin. It is the settled assurance that the One who will judge is the One who already loved us to death and back. You do not need to fear the verdict of a Judge who has already given His life to secure your acquittal.

At the same time, Scripture speaks of a real assessment of the believer's life and works, not to determine salvation but to reveal and reward what was built on the foundation of Christ. Paul says each one's work will be tested by fire, and if it survives, he will receive a reward, but if it is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, only as through fire (1 Corinthians 3:13-15). So the judgment is not a flat formality even for the saved. Our lives matter, our faithfulness matters, what we did with what we were given matters. Grace does not make our choices weightless. It makes them safe enough to be honest about.

So how should you think about being judged. If you are not yet Christ's, the judgment is the most serious news in the world, and the right response is not to manage your fear but to flee to the only one who can stand in your place. If you are His, the final judgment is, strangely, good news, the day evil is finally named and ended, the day every hidden faithfulness is brought to light, the day the Judge who died for you welcomes you home. The same event is terror to the unforgiven and homecoming to the forgiven. The difference is not how good you managed to be. The difference is whose you are when the books are opened.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians broadly affirm a final judgment by Christ, confessed in the creeds, but differ on its details. Catholics hold a particular judgment at death followed by the general judgment, and include purgatory as a purification for the saved before final glory, which Protestants reject. Reformed and Lutheran traditions stress justification by faith alone, so the believer's judgment confirms rather than determines a salvation already secured, with a separate assessment of works for reward. Eastern Orthodoxy emphasizes theosis and is often less juridical in its framing. Christians also disagree over the final state of the unjudged or unevangelized, and over whether the lost suffer eternal conscious punishment, conditional immortality (annihilation), or, as a minority hold, eventual restoration. All affirm Christ as the appointed Judge.

questions.question: Does the fine-tuning of the universe point to God?
questions.shortAnswer: The physical constants that allow life sit inside a startlingly narrow range, and while that does not prove God by force, it makes a Mind behind the cosmos a serious and reasonable inference rather than a desperate one.
questions.answer:
Start with the data, not the conclusion, because the data is what makes this interesting. Physicists across the second half of the twentieth century kept stumbling onto the same uncomfortable fact. The constants that govern our universe, the strength of gravity, the cosmological constant, the ratio of the electromagnetic force to the strong nuclear force, the mass of the electron, appear to be set with a precision that has no obvious reason to be there. Change them by a fraction and you get no stars, no carbon, no chemistry, no observers. Fred Hoyle, an atheist who disliked where the evidence pointed, said it looked as if a superintellect had monkeyed with physics. He was not preaching. He was reading the numbers.

The technical name is fine-tuning, and the honest version of the argument is modest. It does not say the heavens declare a syllogism. It says that of all the ways a universe could have been, the overwhelming majority are sterile, and ours is not, and that asymmetry asks for an account. Three accounts compete. The universe is fine-tuned by necessity (it could not have been otherwise). It is fine-tuned by chance (we happen to have won a cosmic lottery). Or it is fine-tuned by design. The first stalls, because no one has shown why the constants must take the values they do. So the real argument runs between chance and design.

The most popular way to rescue chance is the multiverse. If there are enough universes with enough variation, some will be habitable by sheer statistics, and of course we find ourselves in one of those, because we could not find ourselves anywhere else. That is the anthropic principle, and it is not foolish. But notice what it costs. To avoid one fine-tuner you postulate an unobserved and possibly unobservable infinity of worlds, and the mechanism that generates them, the inflationary field and its parameters, looks suspiciously fine-tuned itself. The philosopher Richard Swinburne and others have argued that design remains the simpler explanation, and simplicity is supposed to be a scientific virtue, not a religious one.

Let me be honest about the limits, because the apologist who oversells this argument deserves the eye-roll he gets. Fine-tuning does not get you to the Father of Jesus Christ. At most it gets you to something like a cosmic intelligence, which is a long way from a God who suffers on a cross. And the design inference can feel like a god-of-the-gaps move, a placeholder we will retract when physics matures. Christians who have lived through enough retracted gaps should hold this loosely.

And yet. There is a difference between a gap in our knowledge and a feature of the structure of reality, and fine-tuning increasingly looks like the second. The deeper physics goes, the more the precision sharpens rather than dissolves. Genesis 1 does not argue this. It assumes it, opening with a God who speaks order out of chaos, who calls light and separates and names. Psalm 19 says the same in poetry, that the sky pours out speech without words. The Christian claim was never that the universe needed God to fill our ignorance. It was that the universe is intelligible at all because Mind precedes matter.

So where does that leave a thoughtful person. Not at the end of an argument, but at the start of a question. If the cosmos is tuned, tuned for what, and by whom, and does that One have anything to say. Fine-tuning can clear the ground. It cannot speak. For speech you have to turn from the heavens to the Word who became flesh, which is exactly the turn John 1 makes, taking the One through whom all things were made and setting him down in a body, in time, in Galilee. The universe whispers that someone is there. Only Christ tells you his name.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians divide over how much weight the fine-tuning argument should carry. Some, in the natural theology tradition of William Lane Craig and the Intelligent Design movement, treat it as strong positive evidence for a designer. Others, often in the BioLogos and Reformed traditions, accept the science but are wary of basing faith on a design inference that future physics might erode, preferring to see fine-tuning as consonant with belief rather than proof of it. A smaller group is comfortable with the multiverse as a live scientific hypothesis and simply denies it threatens faith, since a God who made one universe could as easily make many.

questions.question: Aren't we just our brains? Is there really a soul?
questions.shortAnswer: Neuroscience has shown how deeply mind and brain are entangled, but it has not shown that you are only your brain, and Scripture insists you are a unified creature whose inner life is real, accountable, and held by God beyond the death of your body.
questions.answer:
The honest place to begin is to grant the force of the challenge. We now know that damage to specific regions of the brain changes personality, memory, moral judgment, even the sense of self. Phineas Gage took an iron rod through his frontal lobe and became, by his friends accounts, no longer Gage. A surgeon can stimulate a patch of cortex and produce a memory, a smell, a feeling of the uncanny. The materialist looks at all this and concludes the obvious. There is no ghost in the machine. There is only the machine. If the mind is what the brain does, the soul is a relic we can finally retire.

This deserves more than a flinch. The old picture of the soul as a separate substance loosely parked inside the body, the picture we often inherit from Plato through Descartes, is genuinely hard to square with how integrated we now know we are. A blood-sugar crash can wreck your patience. Grief lives in the body. Christians who treat the soul as the real person and the body as a disposable shell have absorbed more Greek philosophy than Bible, because the scriptural vision of a human being is far more unified than that.

But here is where the materialist conclusion outruns the evidence. The discovery that mind depends on brain is not the discovery that mind is nothing but brain. Correlation and even causation between brain states and mental states does not establish that your experience of red, your sense of obligation, your awareness that you exist, are identical to firing neurons. The philosopher David Chalmers calls this the hard problem of consciousness, and it is hard precisely because no description of the wiring, however complete, seems to add up to what it feels like to be you. Thomas Nagel, an atheist, argued in a famous essay that a purely physical account leaves out the one thing that matters, the inside of experience. The reduction is asserted far more often than it is demonstrated.

There is also a quieter problem for pure materialism, which is that it tends to dissolve the very things we cannot live without. If you are only chemistry running its course, then your reasoning is just the output of physics with no special claim to truth, including the reasoning that led you to materialism. And moral responsibility, the conviction that you ought to have done otherwise, becomes a useful fiction. C. S. Lewis pressed this hard. People who tell us we are only matter still expect us to keep our promises, as if something more than matter were involved.

Scripture does not give us a neuroscience, but it gives us a richer anthropology than either camp. Genesis 2 says God formed the man from dust and breathed life into him, and the man became a living being, a unity, not a soul renting a body. The Hebrew nephesh is closer to a whole living self than to a detachable ghost. Yet the same Scripture insists this self is not exhausted by its biology. Jesus tells us not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot touch the soul (Matthew 10:28), and he promises the dying thief that today he will be with him in Paradise (Luke 23:43). Something of you survives the failure of your brain, held not by its own immortal nature but by the God who made it.

So are you just your brain. No, and the Christian answer is more interesting than the dualism it is usually accused of. You are a creature, embodied through and through, whose conscious, accountable, worshiping life is real and irreducible and known by God. The resurrection of the body, not the escape of the soul, is the Christian hope, which is why Paul in 1 Corinthians 15 stakes everything not on our survival as ghosts but on Christ raised bodily from the grave. You are not a machine. You are not a phantom. You are a person, dust and breath together, and the One who breathed is not finished with you.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Among Christians who all affirm the soul, there is a live debate about its metaphysics. Substance dualists (in the tradition of Augustine, Aquinas, and more recently J. P. Moreland and Richard Swinburne) hold that the soul is a real immaterial substance capable of existing apart from the body between death and resurrection. Christian physicalists and emergent dualists (such as Nancey Murphy and, in a different way, Joel Green) argue that the person is fully embodied and that personal identity is preserved by God's act of resurrection rather than by a freestanding soul. Both camps reject pure materialism and both affirm the resurrection of the body as the final hope.

questions.question: What about near-death experiences? Are they real glimpses of the afterlife?
questions.shortAnswer: Near-death experiences are real experiences that deserve honest attention, but they are not the foundation of Christian hope, which rests not on what a few people report from the edge of death but on Christ who went all the way through it and came back.
questions.answer:
People come to a pastor with these stories more often than you might think, and they come nervous, half expecting to be told they imagined it or that it was demonic. So the first thing to say is that something genuinely happened to them, and dismissing it is neither kind nor honest. Across cultures and decades, a recognizable pattern recurs in people who were close to death and revived. A sense of leaving the body, a tunnel, a light, a figure of overwhelming love, a review of one life, a reluctance to return. Cardiologists like Pim van Lommel and researchers like Raymond Moody and Bruce Greyson have documented thousands of these accounts. They are data. The question is what they are data about.

The skeptical explanation is straightforward and partly persuasive. A dying brain is a stressed brain. Oxygen deprivation, surges of neurochemicals, the firing of the temporal lobe, the release of endorphins, can produce vivid experiences of light, peace, and disembodiment. Pilots in high-g centrifuges report tunnel vision and euphoria. None of that requires an afterlife. The materialist says the brain, shutting down, runs one last spectacular program, and we mistake the screensaver for a window.

But the materialist account has a few stubborn cases it struggles to digest. Some patients report accurate details of the resuscitation room, conversations, instruments, events, during periods when their brains showed little or no measurable activity. The evidence here is contested and easy to overstate, and I will not pretend the case is closed. Honest researchers in the field admit both that the patterns are real and that veridical perception during flat-line states remains hard to verify under controlled conditions. A thoughtful Christian should resist both the eager believer who treats every account as gospel and the reflexive skeptic who has decided in advance what cannot happen.

Here is the deeper pastoral point. Even if every near-death experience were exactly what it seemed, it would still not be the Christian hope, and treating it as such gets the foundation wrong. Notice that these accounts are remarkably plastic. They tend to confirm whatever the person already half believed, and the figure of light is often shaped to the culture. Notice too that they are reports from people who did not actually die in the final sense. They came back. The whole point of the resurrection is that Jesus did not come back from the edge. He came back from the grave, three days in, dead beyond dispute, and he came back not as a vision but in a body people touched and ate with (Luke 24, John 20). Our hope does not rest on the testimony of the briefly-departed. It rests on the eyewitnessed return of the One who went all the way down.

There is also a warning Scripture gives that we should not rush past. Paul says that even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), which is a caution against taking any luminous experience as automatically trustworthy. And the rich man in Jesus parable, begging that someone return from the dead to warn his brothers, is told they have Moses and the prophets, and if they will not hear them they will not be convinced even by one who rises (Luke 16:31). The point is sobering. God has already spoken his decisive word. We are tempted to want the spectacular glimpse instead of the given revelation.

So what do you tell the person across the table. Take their experience seriously, do not explain it away, do not make it carry more than it can. If it left them less afraid of death and more open to God, thank God for that mercy. But anchor them not in their own remarkable night but in the empty tomb, which is public, dated, witnessed, and contested in the open. The glimpse may comfort. Only the resurrection can save. Job, deep in his suffering, did not say he had seen the other side. He said he knew his Redeemer lived and that in his flesh he would see God (Job 19:25-27). That is the ground. Everything else is rumor of a country whose King has already walked back out of its gates.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians range from cautious openness to firm skepticism. Some, including a number of pastors and a few popular books, treat well-attested near-death experiences as genuine if partial encounters with God's presence and signs that consciousness is not merely physical. Others, especially in more cautious evangelical and Reformed circles, worry that such accounts compete with Scripture's sufficiency, can be counterfeited, and feed an appetite for experience over the given word, so they treat them charitably but refuse to build doctrine on them. Nearly all agree the experiences are real psychological events and that the resurrection of Christ, not any individual's testimony, is the basis of Christian hope.

questions.question: Could there be intelligent life on other planets, and would that disprove Christianity?
questions.shortAnswer: Scripture neither asserts nor rules out life elsewhere, and the discovery of intelligent aliens would not disprove the gospel, though it would press Christians to think harder about how the work of Christ relates to the whole of a creation larger than we imagined.
questions.answer:
Let me name the fear under the question, because it is usually a fear and not just curiosity. The worry is that Christianity is a small, parochial story, set on one minor planet around an ordinary star, and that if the universe turns out to be teeming with other minds, the whole drama of Adam and Christ will look like village theater that mistook itself for the cosmos. That worry has a long history. It was raised against the church when Copernicus moved the earth from the center, and the church, to its discredit, sometimes treated astronomical geography as if the faith depended on it. It never did.

Start with what Scripture actually claims and does not. The Bible is relentlessly focused on God, the earth, humanity, and redemption, and it simply does not address the question of other inhabited worlds. That silence is not denial. The ancient writers were not asked, and were not in a position to ask, about exoplanets. To read Genesis as a ban on extraterrestrial life is to demand it answer a question it never raises. At the same time, Scripture loves to multiply God's creatures. The heavens are full of beings we did not invent, the angelic hosts, and the Psalms repeatedly insist that the whole creation, not just our corner, exists to declare God's glory (Psalm 148). A God this lavish with galaxies might well be lavish with life. We do not know.

The scientific picture is genuinely open. There are, by current estimates, on the order of a hundred billion galaxies, each with a hundred billion or so stars, and we now know that planets are common. That is the case for optimism. Against it stands the Fermi paradox, Enrico Fermi's deceptively simple question, if they are out there, where is everybody. The startling silence so far, the absence of any confirmed signal despite decades of listening, is itself data. Some scientists conclude that intelligent life may be vanishingly rare, that the chain of accidents producing a technological civilization is so improbable that we may be effectively alone. The honest answer from both science and theology is the same. We do not yet know.

Now the hard theological question, the one C. S. Lewis took up in a thoughtful essay and in his space trilogy. Suppose there are other rational beings. Would they need redemption. Not necessarily. The Christian story is that sin entered through a free creature's rebellion, not that fallenness is a law of nature. Lewis imagined unfallen worlds that never required a rescue. And if some race had fallen, would Christ have had to die again for them. Scripture gives us a tantalizing hint that the scope of Christ's work is cosmic. Colossians 1 says that through him all things were reconciled, whether things on earth or things in heaven, and Ephesians 1 speaks of God uniting all things in Christ. The cross may be the hinge of a far larger reconciliation than we have imagined, accomplished once, on this planet, with effects we cannot map.

What would actually shake faith is not the existence of aliens but a misplaced assumption about why God came here. The Incarnation does not depend on earth being the biggest or most important place. It depends on God's freedom to stoop wherever he chooses. That the eternal Word took on flesh on a small wet planet is not an embarrassment to be hidden but the very pattern of the gospel, that God comes low, to the overlooked, to the manger and not the throne. A universe full of grander worlds would only deepen the scandal of grace, that he came here.

So would intelligent life elsewhere disprove Christianity. No. It would enlarge it. It might even be one of the most thrilling theological problems the church ever got to think about, and I would rather meet that question with wonder than with defensiveness. The faith has survived being told the earth is not the center of the solar system, and the gospel was never about our cosmic real estate. It was about a cross. Whatever we find out there, the One who made it all is the same One who was nailed to a tree under a Judean sky, and that is not made smaller by a larger universe. It is made larger.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians disagree mostly about implications, not essentials. Some hold that humanity is almost certainly unique, reading the Bible's focus on earth as a strong hint and treating the cosmic silence as confirmation. Others are openly fascinated by the possibility of other life, following C. S. Lewis in speculating about unfallen worlds or about the cosmic reach of Christ's atonement. A few worry the question is a distraction. Across these views there is broad agreement that the discovery of extraterrestrial life would not falsify the gospel, and serious debate would then begin about whether and how the work of Christ extends to other rational creatures.

questions.question: Does the Big Bang fit with Genesis?
questions.shortAnswer: The Big Bang and Genesis agree on the most important thing, that the universe had a beginning and is not eternal, and while they answer different kinds of questions, a thoughtful believer can hold both without strain.
questions.answer:
There is a piece of history here that almost no one knows, and it is worth telling because it cuts against the usual script of science versus faith. The man who first proposed what we now call the Big Bang was a Belgian priest. Georges Lemaitre, a Catholic father and a trained physicist, worked out in the late 1920s that Einstein's equations implied an expanding universe tracing back to what he called the primeval atom, a single point from which everything unfolded. Einstein initially resisted it. It was the believer, not the skeptic, who followed the math to a beginning. The label Big Bang, by the way, was coined as a sneer by Fred Hoyle, who preferred an eternal universe and disliked the theological smell of a cosmic start.

That detail matters because for a long time the prevailing scientific assumption had been a steady-state, eternal cosmos, which sat comfortably with atheism and uncomfortably with Genesis. An eternal universe needs no maker. A universe with an absolute beginning raises, unavoidably, the question of what or who began it. When the evidence for the Big Bang accumulated, the cosmic microwave background discovered in 1965, the redshift of distant galaxies, the abundances of light elements, the science landed on a picture that the opening words of Genesis had asserted all along. In the beginning. There was a beginning. The Hebrew Scriptures had said it for three thousand years.

Now, honesty requires care here, because it is easy to overclaim. Genesis 1 is not a physics paper, and it is a mistake to read the cosmic microwave background out of the Hebrew text or to treat the days of Genesis as a scientific timetable. Genesis is answering a different question than cosmology. Cosmology asks how the universe developed, by what mechanism, on what timeline. Genesis asks who made it, whether it is good, and why we are here. The error of concordism, forcing each verse to match a modern finding, tends to embarrass both the Bible and the science within a generation. Augustine warned about this in the fourth century, long before the conflict, urging Christians not to make fools of themselves by tying Scripture to shaky natural philosophy.

So the deep agreement is not in the details but in the architecture. Both Genesis and modern cosmology say the universe is not self-existent and not eternal. It came to be. The philosopher William Lane Craig has revived an old argument, the kalam, that runs simply. Whatever begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist. Therefore the universe has a cause. The Big Bang does not prove that cause is the God of the Bible, but it removes the eternal-universe escape hatch and leaves the question of a beginner standing in the open, which is exactly where Genesis 1 and John 1 and Hebrews 11 want to put it.

Where genuine debate remains among faithful Christians is over the age of the universe and the timeline of creation, and that debate is real and worth taking seriously rather than papering over. A young-earth reading takes the days as ordinary and the universe as thousands of years old, which puts it in tension with the standard cosmological age of around 13.8 billion years. Old-earth and evolutionary-creation readings take the days as literary or as long ages, and find no conflict between the Big Bang's timeline and a Genesis read for its theological claims. People who love the same Bible land in different places here, and the gospel does not hang on the resolution.

My own counsel is to hold the central thing tightly and the timeline humbly. The central thing is that the cosmos is a creation, spoken into being by a God who is free and good, and that the same God who said let there be light is the God who became flesh and bore a cross. That conviction is not threatened by a universe with a beginning. It is illustrated by one. The believer who first proposed the Big Bang felt no contradiction, and he was closer to both the equations and the text than most of us will ever be. The universe began. Someone began it. Genesis told us who, and the rest of the story tells us what he is like.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The deepest divide is over the age and timeline of creation. Young-earth creationists read the days of Genesis 1 as ordinary days and hold to a universe thousands of years old, regarding the standard cosmological age with suspicion. Old-earth creationists accept the roughly 13.8-billion-year age and read the days as long ages or as a literary framework, seeing the Big Bang as consistent with a creating God. Evolutionary creationists (the BioLogos position) go further, accepting both an old universe and biological evolution as God's means. All three typically agree that the Big Bang's central claim of a cosmic beginning fits the opening conviction of Genesis far better than the eternal-universe alternative it replaced.

questions.question: What are the spiritual disciplines, and where do I start?
questions.shortAnswer: The spiritual disciplines are time-tested practices like prayer, Scripture, fasting, worship, and silence that put you in the place where God can change you, and the best place to start is small, daily, and unglamorous.
questions.answer:
The first thing to get straight is what the disciplines are not, because most people misunderstand them and then either avoid them out of fear or take them up as a performance. The disciplines are not a way to earn God's favor. You already have it in Christ, fully, and no amount of early-morning prayer adds a cent to that account. Nor are they spiritual achievements to log and compare. Dallas Willard, who wrote about this more carefully than almost anyone, defined a discipline as any activity within our power that we engage in to enable us to do what we cannot do by direct effort. You cannot decide to be patient and instantly become patient. But you can do things that, over time, make patience grow in you. The disciplines are the doing of those things.

The historic practices fall roughly into two kinds, and the map Willard drew of them is the one most writers still borrow. There are disciplines of engagement, where you take something up, the study of Scripture, prayer, worship, service, giving, fellowship. And there are disciplines of abstinence, where you let something go, fasting, silence, solitude, simplicity, rest. The second kind is the one our age has nearly lost, and it may be the kind we need most, because a life with no empty spaces in it has no room for God to speak. Jesus himself practiced both. He prayed, he taught, he served, and he withdrew to lonely places, often at great inconvenience, to be alone with the Father (Luke 5:16, Mark 1:35).

Now the honest part, the part the inspirational books skip. Most people who try to start fail within two weeks, and they fail for predictable reasons. They start too big, an hour of prayer when they have never managed five minutes. They start alone, with no one to keep them honest. And they expect to feel something, and when the feeling does not come they conclude it is not working and quit. I have done all three, more than once. The disciplines are not magic, and they will bore you sometimes, and the boredom is not a sign of failure. It is part of the training, the slow unhurrying of a heart that has been formed by a frantic culture to need constant stimulation.

So here is where to actually start, concretely, because vague encouragement helps no one. Begin with two practices, not ten. Take Scripture and prayer, the two oldest and most basic. Read a small portion of the Bible each day, slowly, the Gospel of Mark is a good first place, not to get through it but to let it read you. And pray for a few honest minutes, out loud or written if your mind wanders, which it will. The Psalms can teach you how, because they pray every human emotion, rage and praise and despair and trust, without pretending. Keep the time short enough that you can actually do it tomorrow. Consistency beats intensity every time.

Then build slowly, and build in community. Add one discipline of abstinence within a month or two, a weekly half-day with the phone off, a skipped meal given to prayer, an evening of silence. The reason to involve others is not accountability as guilt but accountability as company. The desert fathers and mothers, who took these practices further than most of us ever will, lived in community precisely because they knew the soul cannot be trusted alone. Find one or two people, or a small group, and tell them what you are attempting.

The goal through all of it is a Person, not a portfolio of habits. Paul's whole aim was to know Christ, and to that end he disciplined himself the way an athlete trains, not to win God's love but because love wants nearness and nearness takes practice (Philippians 3:10, 1 Corinthians 9:24-27). The disciplines are the trellis, not the vine. They do not produce the life. They put you in the sun and the rain where the life can grow. Start small, stay at it past the point where it stops feeling impressive, and let the slow work happen. You are not trying to become spiritual. You are trying to be with God, and these are simply the old, well-worn ways people have learned to do that.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Traditions weight the disciplines differently. Catholic, Orthodox, and Anglican streams give a large place to fixed liturgical prayer, the church calendar, and contemplative practices drawn from the monastic tradition. Many evangelical and Reformed Christians emphasize Scripture, personal and family prayer, and corporate worship, while remaining cautious about certain contemplative techniques (such as some forms of centering prayer) that they fear borrow uncritically from Eastern meditation. Quakers and the holiness traditions have their own emphases on silence and surrender. Beneath the differences there is wide agreement that grace, not effort, saves, and that the disciplines are means God uses rather than works that earn anything.

questions.question: What is fasting for?
questions.shortAnswer: Fasting is voluntarily going without food (or something else) for a time in order to seek God with the whole self, and its purpose is not to twist God's arm but to expose your hungers and turn them toward him.
questions.answer:
Fasting is the most physical of the spiritual disciplines, and that is exactly the point. We are not souls who happen to drag bodies around. We are embodied creatures, and our appetites run deeper into us than we like to admit. To deliberately go hungry is to discover, fast, how much of your life is governed by the management of your cravings, and how thin the membrane is between you and your discontent. By mid-afternoon of a real fast you find out who you are. Irritable, anxious, reaching for distraction. The fast does not create that disorder. It uncovers it, and uncovering is the beginning of healing.

The Bible assumes fasting more than it commands it, which is itself instructive. Jesus did not say if you fast. He said when you fast (Matthew 6:16-18), placing it alongside giving and prayer as a normal part of the life of his followers, and warning only against doing it for an audience. Moses fasted, David fasted, Esther called a fast before risking her life, the early church fasted before sending out Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:2-3). And Jesus himself began his public ministry with forty days of fasting in the wilderness, where the first temptation was precisely about food, about whether he would meet his hunger on his own terms or wait on the Father's word (Matthew 4:1-4). Fasting was the field on which that battle was fought.

So what is it actually for. Several things at once, and it helps to name them honestly rather than reducing fasting to a single technique. It is, first, a way of seeking God with intensity, of saying with the body what the mouth cannot adequately say, that you want him more than you want comfort. It is, second, a way of mourning, of grief and repentance, which is why Scripture so often ties fasting to lament and confession (Joel 2:12). It is, third, a way of standing with the hungry and learning solidarity, of letting your stomach teach you something your full life has hidden. And it is, fourth, a means of focusing prayer in seasons of decision or crisis, when the ordinary diet of life feels like too much noise.

Now let me clear away the most common misuse, because it is everywhere and it is poison. Fasting is not a hunger strike against God, a way to make him act by demonstrating how serious you are. That treats the Father as a reluctant official who responds to pressure, and it is exactly the pagan picture Jesus rejected. God is not moved by your suffering as a transaction. The change fasting works is in you, not in him. It clears the static. It loosens the grip of the appetites that drown out his voice. When the answer comes it comes as gift, not as wages, and the fast simply made you quiet and empty enough to receive it.

There are also wise limits, and a pastor would be failing you not to name them. Fasting from food is not for everyone in every season. Those with histories of disordered eating, those who are pregnant, diabetic, frail, or ill, should not endanger their bodies, and for them fasting from something else, media, noise, a habit, a comfort, can do the same spiritual work. The discipline is the willing surrender of a legitimate good for a season in order to seek God, and there is more than one way to surrender. The Pharisee in Jesus parable fasted twice a week and went home unjustified, because his fasting fed his pride (Luke 18:11-14). The fast that pleases God, Isaiah 58 insists, breaks the yoke of the oppressed and feeds the hungry, never a private performance.

If you have never fasted, start small and start honest. Skip one meal, or one day's eating, and give that time to prayer, and pay attention to what surfaces in you. The discomfort is the curriculum. You will meet your own impatience and your own dependence, and underneath them, if you stay with it, you may meet the One who said that man does not live by bread alone but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. That is the whole of it. Fasting empties the hands so they can be filled with something better than what they were clutching.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on the form and frequency of fasting more than on its value. Catholic and Orthodox traditions observe set fasts tied to the church calendar, such as Lent and weekly abstinence, as part of the rhythm of the year. Many Protestants treat fasting as occasional and Spirit-led rather than scheduled, called for in particular seasons of seeking or crisis. There is also discussion about what may be fasted (food, certain foods, media, comforts) and pastoral debate about how to practice it safely for those with health conditions or eating disorders. Across traditions there is agreement that fasting is a means of grace, not a means of earning God's favor.

questions.question: How do I hear God's guidance for a decision?
questions.shortAnswer: God guides primarily through his word, wise counsel, sanctified reason, and circumstances rather than through a constant inner voice, and for most decisions his will is less a hidden answer to be found than a wise person to become.
questions.answer:
Begin by softening the question, because the way it is usually asked carries a hidden assumption that does more harm than good. People come asking how to find God's will for a decision as if it were a single correct answer hidden somewhere, and the spiritual life were a game of getting warmer or colder until they locate it, with the terror that one wrong move ruins the plan. That picture produces enormous anxiety, and it is largely unbiblical. Garry Friesen and others have pointed out that Scripture rarely describes guidance this way. God is not hiding the answer and scoring you on whether you find it.

What Scripture actually emphasizes is that God's revealed will, the moral and spiritual shape of a faithful life, is already clear and written down, and that most of our decisions are to be made wisely within that frame. Paul does not tell the Thessalonians to discern some secret destiny. He says this is the will of God, your sanctification, your holiness (1 Thessalonians 4:3). Micah does not promise a private revelation. He says God has shown you what is good, to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly (Micah 6:8). The vast majority of what God wants from you in your decision is not hidden at all. It is whether you will be honest, faithful, generous, and humble inside whatever you choose.

For the genuinely open questions, the job, the house, the proposal, where two good options both fit the revealed will, God has given us means of guidance, and it helps to know what they are so you can stop straining for the wrong kind of signal. First and most important is Scripture, soaked in over time, which forms the instincts you will decide with. Second is wise counsel. Proverbs returns to this again and again, that in an abundance of counselors there is safety (Proverbs 11:14, 15:22), and the lone-genius spirituality that bypasses the community is exactly what Proverbs warns against. Third is sanctified reason, the mind God gave you, used prayerfully, weighing the actual goods and costs. Fourth is circumstance, the open and closed doors of providence, read humbly because they are easy to misinterpret. And running through all of it, prayer that asks not mainly for information but for a will surrendered to God's, ready to obey whatever becomes clear.

Now about the inner voice, because this is where people get hurt. God can and sometimes does speak directly, in Scripture and in church history, and I would not dare deny it. But the strong subjective impression, the feeling that God is telling me, is the least reliable of all the means and the easiest to confuse with our own desires, fears, and indigestion. The prophets test for a true word was costly and verifiable, never just an intense feeling (Deuteronomy 18:21-22). So weigh impressions against Scripture and counsel, never above them. A leading that contradicts the Bible is not from God, full stop. A leading that no wise friend can affirm should be held very loosely. Be especially suspicious of the inner voice that conveniently tells you to do exactly what you already wanted.

There is a hard pastoral truth underneath all of this, which is that God often does not give the certainty we crave, and the waiting is part of the formation. He seems far more interested in who you are becoming than in sparing you the discomfort of a real decision made in trust. James says that if anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously (James 1:5), but the promise is wisdom, the capacity to choose well, not a removal of the choosing. The aim is not to be a puppet who needs every step dictated but a mature son or daughter who has so internalized the Father's heart that they can be trusted to decide.

So, practically. Saturate the decision in Scripture and prayer. Get the counsel of people who know you and will tell you the truth. Use your mind honestly, listing the real goods and the real costs. Watch the providences without forcing them. Surrender the outcome in advance, telling God you will go where it becomes clear. And then, having done all that, decide, and walk forward in freedom, trusting that a God who guided you into the deciding will not abandon you in the consequences. Proverbs 3:5-6 does not promise a map. It promises a Guide. Trust him with your whole heart, lean not on your own understanding, acknowledge him in all your ways, and he will make your paths straight, which is to say he will be with you on whatever road you take in faith.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: There is a real divide here. The wisdom view (associated with Garry Friesen and much of the Reformed tradition) holds that for decisions not addressed by Scripture, God expects us to choose wisely within his revealed will, and does not normally give individual hidden answers. The traditional or relationship view (held across charismatic, Wesleyan, and much popular evangelical teaching) holds that God does lead individuals more directly and personally, including through impressions, peace, and promptings of the Spirit, which are to be tested but genuinely expected. Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians give the largest place to prophetic words and inner leading, while cessationist and many Reformed Christians emphasize Scripture, counsel, and providence and treat strong subjective impressions with caution. Nearly all agree that any guidance must be tested against Scripture and that the Bible never contradicts itself.

questions.question: Are angels and demons real?
questions.shortAnswer: Scripture treats angels and demons as real created beings, neither cute nor cartoonish, and the Christian conviction is that the universe is more populated and more contested than the modern imagination allows, without ever giving the dark powers the last word.
questions.answer:
We live between two errors here, and C. S. Lewis named them exactly in the preface to his Screwtape Letters. One is to disbelieve in such beings entirely, treating angels as sentiment and demons as superstition we have outgrown. The other is to believe in them with an unhealthy and excessive interest, seeing a demon behind every flat tire and turning the faith into a fevered drama of spiritual forces. The devil, Lewis said, is equally pleased by both mistakes. The materialist who laughs them off and the obsessive who sees them everywhere have both been maneuvered out of sober reality. The task is to believe what Scripture actually says, no more and no less.

What Scripture says is consistent and unembarrassed. Angels are created spiritual beings, messengers and servants of God, present from the opening pages to the close. They announce, they protect, they worship, they carry out God's purposes (Hebrews 1:14, Psalm 103:20). They are not the souls of the dead, not chubby infants, not romantic guardians of greeting cards. They are powerful, often frightening, and their first words to humans are usually do not be afraid, which tells you something about the experience. And they are servants, never to be worshiped, a point Scripture is careful to make when John falls down before an angel and is sharply told to worship God alone (Revelation 22:8-9).

Demons, in the biblical account, are angelic beings who rebelled, fallen from their place and now set against God and his creatures. Scripture does not give us a detailed origin story, and the popular picture of a war in heaven owes as much to Milton as to the Bible. What it gives us is the reality of a personal evil, an intelligence opposed to God, embodied above all in the figure called the satan, the accuser, the one Jesus called a liar and a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44). The Gospels are full of Jesus confronting these powers directly, casting them out, and it is striking how matter-of-fact he is about it, never lurid, always authoritative. The kingdom of God arrives, in part, as the dispossession of the powers that have held people captive (Luke 11:20).

The modern person rightly worries that all this is pre-scientific, that what the ancients called demonic we now call mental illness or epilepsy, and that diagnosis has often been used to abuse the vulnerable. That worry deserves honesty. The history of treating madness as possession has done real harm, and a wise pastor does not reach for an exorcism when a person needs a doctor. Discernment matters. But notice that the Gospels themselves distinguish between sickness and the demonic, healing the one and casting out the other, rather than collapsing them. And notice too that the confident modern dismissal of all unseen agency is itself a faith claim, the assumption that the closed material world is all there is, which the Christian has good reason to doubt. The point is not to choose between psychiatry and theology but to refuse the flat picture that says only matter is real.

Here is the pastoral center of it, the thing that keeps this from becoming either silly or terrifying. The Christian does not live in fear of the dark powers, because they are defeated powers. Colossians 2 says that on the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, leading them in triumph. The decisive battle is over. What remains is a defeated enemy still capable of harm, like a poison that can sicken but cannot reign. So the New Testament's posture is sober vigilance, not panic. Resist the devil and he will flee (James 4:7). Put on the armor of God (Ephesians 6:11-12). Stand. The verbs are defensive and confident, the posture of people on the winning side mopping up.

So are they real. Yes, and the modern imagination is poorer for forgetting it, having traded a contested, populated, charged universe for a thinner one in which nothing unseen presses on us either to help or to harm. But the Christian who recovers this conviction must hold it the way the New Testament does, with sobriety and not obsession, with vigilance and not fear, and always with the cross in view. The same Jesus who cast out demons with a word now reigns, and the angels who announced his birth still serve the heirs of salvation. We are not alone in the dark. We were never the only ones in the room. And the One who made all of them, seen and unseen, has already won.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians disagree mainly about how active these beings are and how to respond. Charismatic and Pentecostal traditions tend to emphasize ongoing spiritual warfare, deliverance ministry, and direct demonic activity in daily life. Many Reformed, Lutheran, and mainline Christians affirm the reality of angels and demons but place far less emphasis on encounters, stressing instead Christ's decisive victory and the ordinary means of grace. Some thoughtful believers read certain biblical accounts of the demonic as accommodations to ancient understanding, while others take them straightforwardly. Across the spectrum, orthodox Christians affirm that these beings are real creatures, that the dark powers are already defeated at the cross, and that they are never to be feared as if they could overcome God.

questions.question: What is spiritual warfare?
questions.shortAnswer: Spiritual warfare is the Christian's participation in a conflict already won by Christ, fought not against people but against the powers of evil, and waged mainly through truth, prayer, holiness, and faithful endurance rather than through technique or spectacle.
questions.answer:
The phrase has been badly abused, so let me first say what spiritual warfare is not, because the caricatures keep people from the real thing. It is not mainly about dramatic confrontations, rebuking demons by name, claiming territory, or treating every difficulty as a direct satanic attack to be repelled with the right formula. That version, which flourished in certain corners of the church in recent decades, often owes more to a quasi-magical mindset than to Scripture, as if the right words said with enough force could compel the spiritual world. It tends to leave people either puffed up with a sense of cosmic importance or exhausted and afraid. Neither is the New Testament's tone.

The foundational text is Ephesians 6, and what is striking is how sober and almost ordinary it is. Paul says our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities, the powers of this dark world, and spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12). The first move is to relocate the real enemy. The person across the table, the spouse, the colleague, the political opponent, is not the enemy, however much they feel like it. That reframing alone would change most of our conflicts, because we spend our lives at war with people while the actual adversary works precisely by getting us to do that. To name the real enemy is to stop firing on our own.

Then Paul describes the weapons, and they are almost entirely defensive and ethical, which tells you what kind of war this is. The armor is truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer (Ephesians 6:13-18). Notice what is absent. No techniques, no incantations, no map of the demonic hierarchy. The way you resist the powers is by being truthful when lying would be easier, by living rightly when compromise beckons, by trusting God when fear says he has abandoned you, by holding the gospel when despair says it is not true. Spiritual warfare, in its primary biblical sense, looks a great deal like ordinary faithfulness under pressure. The devil's main work is not the spectacular but the slow corrosion of belief, the lie believed, the resentment nursed, the prayer abandoned.

The great theologian of this is Martin Luther, who knew the assaults of the enemy intimately, sometimes too literally. His hymn names the truth exactly. The prince of darkness is real and grim, but one little word shall fell him, because the decisive victory is not ours to win but Christ's already won. This is the engine of all genuine spiritual warfare, and missing it is what makes the counterfeit versions so anxious. We do not fight for victory. We fight from it. The cross has already disarmed the powers (Colossians 2:15). What we do now is stand in a triumph secured by another, the way an army occupies ground its commander has already taken.

There is a real place, I should say, for direct prayer against evil, and the New Testament does not flinch from it. Jesus taught us to pray for deliverance from the evil one (Matthew 6:13). James says resist the devil and he will flee from you, but notice the verse pairs that resistance with submitting to God first (James 4:7), and Peter pairs vigilance against the prowling adversary with humble, sober trust (1 Peter 5:6-9). The order matters. Submission to God, humility, and faith come first. The resisting is real, but it flows from a life already surrendered, not from a technique applied. The Christians most equipped for warfare are usually the least dramatic about it, people of deep prayer and quiet integrity who have learned to recognize the lie when it comes.

So what does it look like in your actual week. It looks like guarding your mind against the lies that accuse and condemn, and answering them with the gospel. It looks like prayer, especially intercession, which is the church's frontline activity. It looks like refusing the resentments and fears the enemy uses as footholds, and forgiving before bitterness can take root (Ephesians 4:26-27). It looks like community, because the Christian alone is the Christian most easily picked off. And it looks like endurance, the unglamorous standing firm that Paul commands four times in one paragraph because that, finally, is the soldier's main job. Not to storm heaven with the right words, but to stand, in the strength of the One who has already won, until the smoke clears and you find you are still on your feet, still believing, still his.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: There is significant difference in emphasis and method. Charismatic and Pentecostal traditions, and the deliverance-ministry movement, give a large and active place to confronting demonic powers directly, including over places and generational patterns. Reformed, Lutheran, and many evangelical Christians read spiritual warfare more soberly as resistance to temptation, deception, and evil through the ordinary means of truth, prayer, holiness, and the word, and are cautious about techniques they see as lacking biblical warrant. Some critique the territorial and strategic-level warfare models as importing extra-biblical ideas. Across the spectrum, Christians agree the conflict is real, the enemy is defeated at the cross, and the believer fights from victory rather than for it.

questions.question: Is it wrong to be wealthy?
questions.shortAnswer: Wealth is not condemned in itself, but Scripture treats it as spiritually dangerous, a stewardship rather than a possession, and the real question is never how much you have but who owns whom.
questions.answer:
Let me start by refusing two easy answers, because both are popular and both are wrong. The first easy answer says wealth is simply a blessing and a sign of God's favor, so the more you have the more God must approve. That is the prosperity gospel, and it is a lie that has wrecked churches and exploited the poor, and Jesus contradicts it flatly when he blesses the poor and warns the rich (Luke 6:20-24). The second easy answer says wealth is simply evil and the faithful must all be poor. That too misreads the Bible, which never commands universal poverty and includes among the faithful people of real means, Abraham, Job, Lydia, Joseph of Arimathea. The truth is harder and more uncomfortable than either, and it will not let any of us off the hook.

What Scripture actually says is that wealth is not wrong but it is dangerous, the way fire is not wrong but will burn down your house if you are careless with it. Paul writes that the love of money, not money itself, is a root of all kinds of evil, and that some, eager for it, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs (1 Timothy 6:10). The danger is not in the bank account but in the heart's attachment to it. Jesus said it is hard, hard, for a rich person to enter the kingdom, harder than a camel through a needle's eye (Mark 10:23-25), not because money is dirty but because it is a rival god, the most plausible alternative to dependence on the real one. You cannot serve God and money, he said, naming money almost as a deity with a will of its own.

Why is it so dangerous. Because wealth lies to you about your condition. It tells you that you are secure when you are not, that you need nothing when you are as needy as anyone, that you have earned what was in fact given. The church in Laodicea said it was rich and needed nothing, and Christ told it that it was wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked, and did not know it (Revelation 3:17). That is the peculiar peril of comfort, that it anesthetizes the very ache that would drive us to God. The poor man knows he is dependent. The rich man has to be told, and usually does not want to hear it. This is why Jesus warned the prosperous more sharply than almost anyone else.

The reframe that changes everything is stewardship. In the biblical view you do not own your wealth. God does, and you are a manager who will give an account (Luke 16:1-13, Matthew 25:14-30). That single shift dissolves both the pride of the rich and the resentment of the poor, because it makes the question not how much do I have but what am I doing with what I have been entrusted. The rich are not condemned for being rich but warned not to be haughty, to set their hope not on uncertain riches but on God, and to be rich in good deeds, generous, ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17-19). The measure of a Christian's relationship to wealth is generosity, and specifically generosity toward the poor, which Scripture treats not as optional charity but as basic justice and a test of whether the love of God actually dwells in us (1 John 3:17).

Now let me be honest and self-implicating, because it is easy to preach this from a comfortable life, and I do. Most of us reading this are, by any global or historical measure, wealthy beyond the dreams of nearly everyone who has ever lived, and we do not feel rich because we compare upward, always to those with more. That comparison is itself part of the deception. The first step toward faithfulness is simply to tell the truth about where we stand, to stop pretending we are the struggling ones, and to feel the weight of how much has been entrusted to us. The young ruler walked away sad because he had great wealth and could not loosen his grip (Mark 10:22). The question Jesus put to him is the question put to every one of us. Not whether we will become destitute, but whether the thing we are clutching has become the thing that owns us.

So, is it wrong to be wealthy. No. It is wrong to trust wealth, to hoard it, to let it make you blind and proud and forgetful of the poor, and the trouble is that wealth pulls toward all of those by gravity, quietly, while you tell yourself you are fine. The faithful wealthy person is the one who holds money with an open hand, gives generously and gladly, lives more simply than they could, and keeps their security fixed on God rather than on the balance. Zacchaeus, when Christ entered his house, gave half his goods to the poor and repaid fourfold all he had cheated, and Jesus said salvation had come to that house (Luke 19:8-9). Notice he did not become destitute. He became free. That is the goal. Not poverty for its own sake, but a heart so loosened from money that it can finally hold the only treasure that lasts.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ over how radical the call must be. The prosperity gospel (widely rejected by mainstream theologians) treats wealth as a sign of faith and God's favor. At the other end, radical-discipleship and many Anabaptist voices, along with figures in the simple-living and liberation traditions, read Jesus' words as a call to genuine renunciation, voluntary poverty, or community of goods. The broad middle, across Catholic, Reformed, and evangelical teaching, affirms private property and the legitimacy of wealth held as stewardship, while insisting on generosity, simplicity, justice for the poor, and vigilance against greed.
