The debate is real about how much is too much, but there is wide agreement that the love of money is spiritually deadly and that care for the poor is not optional.

questions.question: What does the Bible actually teach about sex?
questions.shortAnswer: The Bible treats sex as a good gift of God, neither shameful nor ultimate, given its proper home in the covenant of marriage, where it is meant to express and deepen a lifelong, exclusive union of two whole persons.
questions.answer:
The first thing to clear away is the assumption that the Bible is embarrassed about sex or hostile to it, because that assumption is so widespread and so wrong. It is not the Bible but a later, half-pagan strain in Christian history that taught suspicion of the body. Scripture opens with God creating humanity male and female, calling them to become one flesh, and pronouncing the whole thing very good, before any fall, any shame (Genesis 1:27-31, 2:24-25). There is an entire book of the Bible, the Song of Songs, devoted to the unembarrassed celebration of erotic love between a husband and wife. The biblical writers thought sex was a gift, powerful and beautiful, made by a God who is not a prude. Any account that misses this has not read the text.

But the same Scripture that affirms sex so highly also fences it, and the modern reader needs to understand why before dismissing the boundaries as repression. The Bible's consistent teaching is that sex belongs within marriage, the covenant union of a man and a woman, and that this is its proper and only home (Genesis 2:24, Hebrews 13:4). The reason is not that sex is too dirty to be enjoyed freely but, almost the opposite, that it is too significant to be treated casually. Scripture treats sex as a kind of language, a body saying what the covenant means, I am wholly and permanently yours. To say that with the body while withholding it in the commitment is, in the biblical view, a kind of lie the flesh tells. That is what Paul is getting at when he insists that sexual union is never merely physical, that it joins persons at a level deeper than we pretend (1 Corinthians 6:16-18).

This is why the Bible takes sexual sin seriously, not because it is the worst of sins but because it involves the whole self in a way few other acts do. Paul tells the Corinthians, living in a city as sexually permissive as any modern one, that the body is not meant for immorality but for the Lord, that it is a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:13-20). The point is dignity, not disgust. Your body matters. What you do with it matters. The pagan view, ancient and modern, treats sex as either trivial appetite or ultimate fulfillment, and the Bible refuses both. It is neither nothing nor everything. It is a good gift with a given shape.

Let me name honestly where this collides with our culture, because pretending the collision is small helps no one. The modern sexual ethic is built on consent and authenticity, the idea that what consenting adults do is no one's business and that to deny a desire is to deny the self. The biblical ethic agrees that consent is necessary but denies that it is sufficient, and it flatly rejects the notion that our desires define us or must be obeyed. Jesus located sexual sin not only in acts but in the heart, in lust that uses another person in the imagination (Matthew 5:27-28), which means none of us comes to this subject clean, and that is exactly the point. The Bible's sexual ethic is not a club the chaste use to beat the unchaste. It is a standard under which every one of us stands convicted and in need of grace.

Which brings me to the gospel dimension, because a sexual ethic without grace is just law, and law cannot heal what is broken here. Scripture is unflinching about sexual sin and also astonishingly tender toward sexual sinners. Jesus did not condemn the woman caught in adultery, though he did not pretend her act was nothing either, he told her to go and sin no more, holding truth and mercy together (John 8:11). The woman at the well, with her five husbands, became the first evangelist in her town (John 4). The whole drama of redemption is told, again and again, as a marriage, God the faithful husband to an unfaithful people, which means our sexual faithfulness or failure is woven into the deepest picture of what God is like and what he has done.

So what does the Bible actually teach. That sex is good, made by God, and meant for marriage, where two people give themselves wholly and permanently to each other and the body finally tells the truth the covenant has promised. That it is neither shameful nor salvific, neither dirty nor divine, but a gift with a shape, and that the shape is for our flourishing and not our frustration. And that all of us, married and single, faithful and fallen, come to this subject as people who have failed somewhere, in act or thought, and who therefore need not first a higher standard but a Savior. The good news is that there is one, and that he meets people precisely at their place of deepest shame, and does not leave them there.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Within historic Christianity there is broad agreement that sex is a good gift reserved for marriage, but real differences on surrounding questions. Traditions differ on contraception (Catholic teaching restricts it, while most Protestants permit it), on the place and value of singleness and celibacy (held especially high in Catholic and Orthodox tradition), and on pastoral questions like how to counsel those who have already crossed these lines. There are also debates about the relative seriousness of various sexual sins and about how strictly the church should discipline them. More recently some progressive Christians have argued for revising the traditional ethic, while the historic and global church has overwhelmingly maintained it. This page keeps to the general teaching shared across the historic traditions.

questions.question: Is living together before marriage wrong?
questions.shortAnswer: Scripture reserves sexual union and the shared life it signifies for marriage, so cohabitation as a substitute for or trial run at marriage falls short of that pattern, though the pastoral response should aim at the heart and the goal, not just the arrangement.
questions.answer:
Let me begin where most people actually are, because this question is rarely asked in the abstract. It is usually asked by someone already living with a partner, or about to, who loves God or is drawn to him, and who is bracing to be condemned. So I want to be careful to tell the truth without reaching for a stone. The honest biblical answer is that the arrangement, as it is usually meant, does fall short of God's design, and pretending otherwise would not be love. But how we get there, and what we do with it, matters enormously, and a pastor who leads with judgment has already failed.

The biblical foundation is the one we have seen elsewhere. Scripture reserves sexual union for marriage, the covenant of a man and a woman, and treats that union as a body-language of total, permanent self-gift (Genesis 2:24, Hebrews 13:4, 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5). Cohabitation, in the way our culture means it, typically involves sexual union without that covenant, the intimacy of marriage without its commitment, and that is precisely the gap Scripture addresses. The body is saying I am wholly and permanently yours while the will is saying not yet, maybe, we will see. There is an incoherence in it, and underneath the practical questions that is the real one. Living together usually means living as married while withholding the very thing that makes a marriage, the public, permanent, before-God-and-witnesses promise.

It is worth noticing that the social-science data, gathered by researchers with no theological stake, has turned out to be sobering for the most common justification. The strongest argument for cohabitation has always been that it is a sensible trial run, a way to test compatibility before the big commitment. But decades of study have found, at best, no protective effect and often the opposite, that couples who cohabit first do not generally end up with stronger marriages, and many drift into marriage by inertia rather than choosing it. The sociologists call it sliding rather than deciding. People move in for convenience and convenience hardens into a marriage no one quite chose. The trial-run logic, which sounds so wise, tends not to deliver what it promises, and the Bible's instinct that commitment should precede the shared life turns out to have practical wisdom in it.

That said, I want to resist a reflex in the church that is its own kind of failure. We have sometimes treated cohabitation as if it were the unforgivable sin, the one thing that makes a couple unwelcome, while waving through the gossip, greed, and pride sitting comfortably in the pews. That is hypocrisy, and Jesus reserved his hardest words not for the sexually broken but for the religiously self-righteous (Matthew 23). A couple living together who walk into a church are not enemies to be repelled. They are people to be loved toward something better, and the something better is not mainly a change of address but a change of heart that wants what God wants. The goal is never just to get them into separate apartments. It is to draw them toward the whole vision of covenant love that their arrangement is an unfinished version of.

So what counsel actually helps. For a couple who want to follow Christ, the path is not condemnation but a clear and gracious call toward the real thing, which usually means either marrying or, in the meantime, restructuring the relationship so that it honors God rather than improvising marriage. That is hard and costly, and it should be honored as costly rather than demanded glibly. I have watched couples make that change at real expense, financial and social and emotional, and it is one of the more beautiful things a pastor gets to witness, two people choosing to do it God's way precisely when it is inconvenient. The question to put to them is not are you sinning but what do you actually want, the half-measure or the whole gift.

And here, as everywhere in this terrain, the last word has to be grace, because law alone will only produce either despair or hypocrisy. None of us comes to the subject of sex and marriage with clean hands, and the gospel is not a reward for those who got it right but a rescue for those who did not. Whatever a person's history, whatever the current arrangement, the door is open, and Christ specializes in meeting people exactly where their lives are tangled and untangling them with more patience than we expect. The call to leave the half-version behind is real, but it is a call into freedom and toward a love that keeps its promises, issued by the One who has kept every promise to us. That is not a burden laid on people. It is an invitation held out to them.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians who share the traditional ethic still differ pastorally. Some churches treat cohabitation as a clear barrier to membership, leadership, or marriage in the church until it is resolved, emphasizing accountability. Others take a more gradual, relational approach, welcoming cohabiting couples and walking with them toward marriage or change over time. There is also debate about engaged couples and about cultures where formal marriage is delayed for economic reasons. A minority of progressive Christians question the traditional ethic itself. Across the historic traditions, however, there is broad agreement that sexual union belongs in marriage and that cohabitation as a substitute for covenant falls short of that pattern.

questions.question: What does the Bible say about divorce and remarriage?
questions.shortAnswer: The Bible holds marriage to be a lifelong covenant and treats divorce as a grievous breaking of it, while recognizing certain grounds on which it may be permitted, and it speaks to the divorced with both honesty and deep mercy.
questions.answer:
This is a subject where the church has often managed to be both too lax and too cruel, sometimes at the same time, and I want to handle it with the care it deserves, because behind the question are almost always real wounds. People asking about divorce are rarely curious. They are bleeding, or guilty, or afraid, or all three. So let me try to tell the truth plainly and then hold that truth the way Jesus did, with full honesty and full mercy, never trading one for the other.

Start with God's design, because everything else is a departure from it. Jesus, asked about divorce, went back behind the Mosaic law to the beginning, to the one-flesh union of Genesis, and said what God has joined together, let no one separate (Matthew 19:4-6). Marriage in the biblical vision is a covenant, not a contract, a lifelong, exclusive bond meant to image God's own faithfulness to his people. That is the high ground, and we should not lower it. Divorce is never presented as good, never as the design, never as something God delights in. The prophet Malachi puts it starkly, that God hates the treachery of divorce because it tears apart what was meant to be one (Malachi 2:16). Any honest treatment has to begin by feeling the weight of that, the genuine tragedy of a covenant broken.

But the same Jesus who raised the standard also recognized that we live in a fallen world where covenants are broken, and he and the apostles named grounds on which divorce, while still a grief, may be permitted. Jesus allowed it in the case of sexual unfaithfulness, porneia, the betrayal of the one-flesh union at its core (Matthew 19:9). Paul, addressing a different situation, allowed that if an unbelieving spouse abandons a believer, the believer is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15). Many faithful interpreters have understood these as windows into a principle rather than an exhaustive list, that when one party has already fundamentally shattered the covenant, through betrayal or desertion, the innocent party is not held to a bond the other has destroyed. And most pastors and theologians, reading these texts together with the whole of Scripture's care for the vulnerable, have concluded that abuse, which is its own grave form of covenant treachery and a threat to safety, must be taken with the same seriousness. No one should be told that God requires them to remain in danger.

Remarriage is the harder edge of the question, and here too the Bible is neither permissive nor merciless. Where a divorce was on biblically recognized grounds, the historic and majority Christian view has been that remarriage is permitted, that the innocent party is free (1 Corinthians 7:15, 7:27-28). Where a divorce was not on such grounds, the question becomes more painful, and Christians have differed sincerely. What unites the faithful positions is the refusal to treat remarriage as either automatic or impossible, the insistence that each situation be weighed with both the standard and the mercy in view, and the conviction that God's grace reaches even into the wreckage of our worst failures.

Let me speak directly to the divorced person reading this, because the doctrine can land as a verdict when it is meant to be a framework. If your marriage ended, even if you bear real responsibility for it, you are not beyond the reach of God. Divorce is not the unforgivable sin, and the church that has treated it as a permanent mark of shame has misrepresented its Lord. The Jesus we meet in the Gospels spoke with the woman at the well, who had been through five marriages, not with contempt but with an offer of living water (John 4). David committed adultery and worse and remained a man after God's heart, not because his sin was small but because his repentance was real and God's mercy was larger. Whatever your history, there is a way forward, and it begins not with despair but with honesty before a God who already knows and already loves.

So what does the Bible say. That marriage is a lifelong covenant and ought to be fought for, that divorce is always a tragedy and never God's design, that there are nonetheless circumstances in which it may be permitted because the covenant has already been broken by betrayal, desertion, or abuse, and that those who have been through it are met by God with mercy rather than rejection. The aim of all this is not to make people miserable in bad marriages or ashamed of failed ones. It is to honor what marriage is, to protect the vulnerable within it, and to extend grace to everyone, married and divorced and remarried, who has discovered how heavy and how holy this covenant really is. Hold the standard high. Hold the people gently. Jesus did both, and so must we.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: This is one of the most genuinely contested areas of Christian ethics. The no-divorce-no-remarriage view (held by some Catholics in practice through annulment, and by some conservative Protestants) treats marriage as indissoluble while one spouse lives. The traditional Protestant view permits divorce and remarriage on the grounds of adultery and desertion (the so-called Erasmian view, drawn from Matthew 19 and 1 Corinthians 7). A broader view extends the recognized grounds to include abuse and other grave covenant-breaking. Catholic teaching distinguishes annulment (a declaration the marriage was never valid) from divorce. Christians who hold these views in good faith all affirm marriage as a covenant meant for life, all grieve divorce as a tragedy, and increasingly agree that the church must protect victims of abuse rather than bind them to danger.

questions.question: Does prayer actually change God's mind?
questions.shortAnswer: Scripture shows God relenting when people pray, and it declares that God does not change. The traditions hold those texts together in different ways, and every one of them agrees the praying is not theater.
questions.answer:
Set the two stacks of texts side by side, because the puzzle is in the Bible before it is in your head. One stack says God does not change. I the Lord do not change, says Malachi. God is not a man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind, says Numbers. The other stack shows him changing course at human petition. Moses pleads on the mountain and the Lord relented from the disaster he had spoken. Hezekiah, told by a prophet that he would die, prays against the wall and receives fifteen more years. Nineveh repents and the threatened ruin does not fall. A doctrine built on either stack alone will be tidy and false.

The classical answer, held by most of the church across its history, is that God ordains ends and means together. From eternity God purposed to spare Nineveh through Jonah's preaching and Nineveh's repenting, to heal Hezekiah through Hezekiah's praying. Prayer changes things, really and causally, because God wove the asking into the way his unchanging purposes arrive. The relenting texts, on this reading, describe a changeless character meeting changed people, the way the same sun melts wax and hardens clay.

Not all Christians are satisfied with that. Open theists take the relenting texts at face value and hold that God, having chosen to make free creatures, genuinely responds within a future he has left partly open. Molinists propose that God, knowing what every free creature would do in every possible circumstance, arranged a world in which your prayer and its answer fit his plan without forcing either. These are real differences, and the doctrine page gives each its strongest case. But stand back and notice what every view affirms. Prayer is causal. Things happen because people ask that would not otherwise happen. You do not have, James says flatly, because you do not ask.

Which means the practical answer is the one Jesus gave, not a theory but a command. Ask. The Bible spends almost no time explaining how prayer works and enormous time insisting that it does.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The divide is the one the doctrine page maps. Classical theists, the broad tradition, hold exhaustive foreknowledge and an unchanging counsel, with prayer as an appointed means inside it. Open theists hold that the future is partly open and God genuinely responds, at the cost of classical foreknowledge. Molinists hold a middle knowledge that secures both sovereignty and freedom, at the cost of considerable complexity. All three affirm petition wholeheartedly. The pastoral differences surface in how each speaks about unanswered prayer, and a separate entry takes that grief seriously on its own terms.

questions.question: What is the unforgivable sin, and have I committed it?
questions.shortAnswer: Jesus named one sin that will not be forgiven, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and the context defines it. The tormenting fear that you have committed it is, by that very context, strong evidence that you have not.
questions.answer:
Few verses have produced more midnight terror, so put the text on the table. Scribes from Jerusalem watched Jesus free the afflicted and explained it away with the verdict that he cast out demons by the prince of demons. Jesus answered that every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven, even words spoken against the Son of Man himself, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness. Mark adds the interpreting line, for they were saying he has an unclean spirit. In its own context, the unforgivable sin is not a stray word, a doubt, a season of rebellion, or an intrusive thought in an anxious mind. It is the settled, eyes-open verdict that the Spirit's work in Christ is demonic. Light called darkness by people who saw the light clearly and preferred the dark.

Notice why that sin, uniquely, has no forgiveness. Not because God's mercy hits a limit, but because this sin walls off the road mercy travels. The Spirit is the one who convicts, softens, and draws a person to Christ. To finally and knowingly call that very voice satanic is to cut the telephone line and then never hear the phone. It is unforgivable the way a disease that destroys the ability to swallow cannot be cured by medicine taken by mouth. The hardening is the sentence.

Now the pastoral word the old divines gave consistently. The person tormented by fear of having committed this sin is displaying the exact opposite of its symptoms. Dread of losing God is the Spirit's fingerprint, not his absence. The scribes in Mark 3 were not lying awake grieved. They were satisfied. If you were hardened, your hardness would not hurt. Every historic tradition, whatever else it disputes, has told anxious consciences the same thing here, that the desire to be forgiven is itself evidence the door stands open, and that if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us.

So the answer has an edge and a comfort, and both are the text's. There is a way of seeing that ends in night. And the fact that you are asking, afraid, is daylight.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Traditions debate the edges. Some connect this passage to the apostasy warnings of Hebrews 6 and 10 and ask whether a true believer can arrive at such hardening, a question tangled with the perseverance debate. Reformed theology holds that the elect never finally commit it. Arminians hold that a person can, by persistent resistance, sear the conscience past return. Catholic teaching treats final impenitence, refusing mercy to the very end, as the sin's ultimate form. All agree on the pastoral floor, that this text was never given to torment the tender, and that no one grieving over sin has committed the sin that cannot grieve.

questions.question: Why does God allow earthquakes and tsunamis?
questions.shortAnswer: Free will explains cruelty. It does not explain plate tectonics. Scripture offers a groaning creation and a Lord who refused to read disasters as verdicts, and it leaves a remainder no honest theology hides.
questions.answer:
Human evil has a suspect. When we ask why there are wars, the free-will answer at least names the criminal. But no one chose the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 or the Boxing Day tsunami of 2004. The fault lines were laid down before any human sinned a sin, and the suffering they cause falls on the just and the unjust with meteorological indifference. Philosophers call this natural evil, and it is the harder half of the problem. Voltaire wrote a whole poem against easy optimism after Lisbon, and he was right that the pat answers died in that rubble.

Jesus was asked the question in nearly modern form. A tower in Siloam had collapsed and killed eighteen people, and the crowd wanted the moral calculus explained, whose sin had earned it. He refused the whole framework. Those eighteen, he said, were not worse offenders than anyone else in Jerusalem. He cut the wire between disaster and divine verdict, and any theology that reads hurricanes as targeted punishments has to walk over his answer to do it.

What Scripture does offer is stranger and larger. Paul describes creation itself as subjected to futility, groaning as in childbirth, awaiting a liberation that has not yet come. The world we inhabit is good and not yet finished, glorious and out of joint, and Christians have read its disorder as connected, in ways beneath our sight, to the larger rupture between creation and its Maker. Some add the sober physical fact that the same tectonics that break cities also built the continents and keep the planet habitable, a world of real process rather than painted scenery. Those thoughts explain something. No one should pretend they explain a drowned village.

The Christian answer finally stands on two facts rather than an equation. God entered the groaning world himself and died in its violence. And the same Bible that admits the sea's chaos promises a morning when the sea is no more and every tear is wiped away. Between those two facts the church does its work, which after every earthquake has looked like digging.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on the mechanism. Some trace natural evil to the fall, holding that human sin fractured the created order itself. Others hold that a dynamic creation with real physical freedom was always the kind of world God chose to make, and that its dangers are the price of its fruitfulness. Still others appeal to the disruption of rebellious spiritual powers, and many simply file the question under mystery held in trust. The traditions also divide over whether God specifically ordains each disaster or permits a general order, the same fault line that runs through the providence debates.

questions.question: If God knew evil would come, why create the world at all?
questions.shortAnswer: Dostoevsky's Ivan asked it best, and the Bible never answers it directly. What it shows instead is a God who priced the world's evil into his own flesh before the foundation of the world.
questions.answer:
This may be the heaviest question a human being can ask, and the most serious novelist ever to face it put it in its sharpest form. Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov does not deny God. He returns the ticket, saying that if the world's final harmony costs the torture of one child, the price is too high. Read that chapter before you answer anyone. A faith that has not felt its force has no business replying to it, and the Bible itself never explains why God, foreseeing everything, still said, let there be.

A few honest observations can be made from inside. First, the alternatives are not obviously better. A world with no freedom would have no evil and no love either, only machinery running in the dark with no one to be glad of it. And never to have existed is a strange gift to prefer. Few who press the argument would hand their own children over to it. Second, the ledger is not closed. Judging a world that Scripture insists is unfinished is like judging a symphony from its darkest bar. Paul, who suffered more than most of his critics, wrote that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed. That is either the cruelest sentence in the Bible or the truest, and which it is depends entirely on whether the resurrection happened.

But the specifically Christian answer is neither of those. It is that God did not price the world's evil onto his creatures and stand clear. The New Testament says the Lamb was foreknown before the foundation of the world, the rescue planned before the wound. God created knowing what it would cost, and knowing that the one it would cost most was himself. Whatever that leaves unexplained, and it leaves much, it forever forbids one picture, the God who risked nothing and billed us for everything.

So the question stands, and it stands changed. You are no longer asking why a spectator permitted a tragedy. You are asking why the playwright wrote himself into the dying. And to that question the Bible does give its one-word answer. Love.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The traditions frame God's purpose differently. Reformed theology holds that God ordained the whole, fall included, for the fullest display of his glory and grace, a reading connected to the old phrase felix culpa, the fortunate fall. Arminians hold that love required genuine freedom and freedom carried genuine risk. Open theists go further and say the future was truly open, so God knew evil as possibility rather than certainty. Molinists say God chose, among all feasible worlds of free creatures, the one whose whole story serves his good ends. Each view guards something real, and each pays a cost the others are quick to name.

questions.question: What happens to babies who die?
questions.shortAnswer: Scripture gives no single verse that settles it, and the church has answered with hope in almost every generation. David's word over his dead son, I shall go to him, is where most Christians have rested.
questions.answer:
First, if you are asking because of a child you lost, you need the pastoral word before the doctrinal one. Nothing in Scripture, and nothing in the character of God, gives you reason to fear for your child. The theologians who differ on nearly everything else have converged here with striking consistency. Now the honest account of why.

Scripture never addresses the question in a direct sentence, and honesty starts there. What it gives is a handful of load-bearing texts. David, after his infant son died, said, I shall go to him, but he will not return to me, and said it as comfort, expecting reunion. Jesus took children in his arms and said the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these, and Luke notes that people were bringing him even infants. Deuteronomy speaks of children who have no knowledge of good or evil, marking out a real category of those who never reached moral agency. And Abraham's question rings over the whole matter, shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? The Judge will not need our excuses made for him.

From those texts the church built its hopes by different routes. Many evangelicals speak of an age or condition of accountability, holding that God does not condemn those incapable of moral response. The Westminster Confession states that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ, and Charles Spurgeon, no soft sentimentalist, preached infant salvation outright. Rome once speculated about limbo, but it was never dogma, and in 2007 the Vatican's own theological commission concluded there are serious grounds to hope that infants who die without baptism are saved. Across its deepest divisions, the church leans the same direction.

What no serious tradition teaches is presumption the other way. The strong consensus is grace. Children who died before they could choose anything are precisely the case for which the mercy of God, purchased at the cross, is most confidently trusted.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The differences concern grounds more than outcome. Reformed Christians rest the hope on election and covenant promise rather than innocence, since they hold that all inherit Adam's fall. Wesleyans rest it on prevenient grace covering those who cannot respond. Catholics rest it on the mercy of God and the church's desire in baptism's absence. A few voices in history, Augustine the weightiest, argued harder lines about unbaptized infants, and some traditions refuse to speculate past what is written. No major communion today teaches that God condemns those incapable of faith as though they had refused it.

questions.question: The Gospels are copies of copies. How is that trustworthy?
questions.shortAnswer: The telephone-game picture is the wrong model. Transmission was written, branching, and massively duplicated, which means errors get caught by comparison instead of compounding down a single line.
questions.answer:
Get the concession on the table first. No original manuscript of any New Testament book survives. What we have are copies of copies, made by hand, and the copyists made mistakes. Scribes skipped lines, misheard dictation, harmonized one Gospel toward another, and occasionally smoothed a reading they found awkward. Counted across every manuscript, the differences run into the hundreds of thousands. If the text really had been whispered down a telephone line for centuries, distrust would be the only honest response.

But the telephone game is the wrong picture, and the difference is everything. In the game, each hearer destroys the previous message, one fragile line with no checking. Manuscript transmission was written, not whispered, and it branched like a family tree rather than running single file. Copies multiplied across Egypt, Syria, North Africa, and Italy within a few generations, so an error born in one branch appears nowhere else, which is precisely how scholars catch it. More than five thousand Greek manuscripts survive, along with early translations and heavy quotation in other ancient writers, a body of evidence no other ancient text approaches. A famous fragment of John kept in Manchester is commonly dated to the first half of the second century, within a few decades of the Gospel's composition. For most classical authors, the gap between original and first surviving copy is measured in centuries.

As for those variants, the overwhelming majority are spelling slips and word-order changes that no translation could even show you. The two largest genuinely disputed passages, the longer ending of Mark and the story of the woman caught in adultery, sit flagged in the footnotes of any modern Bible, which is the opposite of a cover-up. Even Bart Ehrman, the best-known skeptical textual critic alive, has granted in print that no essential Christian belief rests on a disputed reading.

So here is the honest statement. You are not reading a photocopy of the originals. You are reading a text reconstructed from an enormous, early, geographically scattered family of witnesses, with the uncertain places marked in the margin for your inspection.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ over method more than over confidence. Most scholars practice reasoned eclecticism, weighing each variant by the age and spread of its witnesses. A minority argues for Byzantine priority, trusting the majority text the church copied for a thousand years. A smaller confessional group holds to the Textus Receptus behind the Reformation Bibles, convinced that God preserved his word in the text the church actually used. And some inside the academy press the skeptical challenge that what we possess is the church's text rather than the apostles' autographs. The doctrine page lays out all four positions at full strength.

questions.question: Who decided which books belong in the Bible?
questions.shortAnswer: No council voted the Bible into existence. The canon grew the way a family recognizes its own voice, over generations, with real debate at the edges, and the debated edges are worth knowing about.
questions.answer:
The suspicious version of the story is well known. Powerful bishops, centuries after Jesus, chose the books that served them and buried the rest. And there are true facts underneath the suspicion. The list did take centuries to settle. Some books now in your Bible, Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, Jude, Revelation, were doubted by serious Christians for generations. Others, like the Shepherd of Hermas, were read in churches and finally left out. Anyone who tells you the canon dropped from heaven bound in leather is skipping the human history.

But the conspiracy version gets the mechanics wrong. The Council of Nicaea in 325 did not discuss the canon at all, whatever the novels say, and there was no single vote anywhere. The four Gospels and Paul's letters were functioning as Scripture remarkably early, quoted as authoritative within a generation or two of the apostles, and 2 Peter already sets Paul's letters alongside the other Scriptures. The Muratorian fragment, a list most scholars date to the late second century, already names the bulk of our New Testament. The first surviving list matching our twenty-seven books exactly comes in an Easter letter of Athanasius in 367. The later councils ratified what scattered congregations on three continents had already been reading for generations. Recognition is the honest word, not selection.

And the tests were public. Was the book apostolic, written by an apostle or a close companion? Was it received everywhere, not the property of one region or faction? Did it square with the faith the apostles had taught openly from the beginning? The later Gnostic gospels were not suppressed rivals. They were latecomers, written generations after the events, and the churches knew it.

As for the Old Testament, Christians received it rather than chose it. Jesus cited the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms as the Scriptures his own life answered to. The church did not assemble a Bible and then believe it. It was born holding one.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The genuine live divide is the Apocrypha, the books written between the testaments. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include them as deuterocanonical Scripture, citing the church's long liturgical use and the Greek Bible of the earliest Christians. Protestants hold the shorter Hebrew canon, noting that Jesus and the apostles never cite those books as Scripture and that Jerome himself set them apart. Beneath that sits a deeper question of authority, whether the church's recognition of the canon places the church over the list or under the books. The doctrine pages on the two canons and the Apocrypha work through all of it.

questions.question: Does archaeology support the exodus, or disprove it?
questions.shortAnswer: Neither, cleanly. There is no direct Egyptian record of Israel leaving, and there are background details the story gets strikingly right. Honest people weigh the same evidence differently, and both scales belong on the table.
questions.answer:
Say the hard part plainly. No Egyptian inscription mentions Israelite slaves departing, no pharaoh records losing an army in the sea, and generations of digging in the Sinai have produced no campsite trail for a great migration. Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman, in The Bible Unearthed, argue from that silence that the exodus story as written is a much later composition serving later national needs. A believer who never hears this stated honestly will eventually hear it stated hostilely, so hear it here first.

Now the other scale. Egyptian records almost never preserve defeats, and the mudbrick cities of the delta have mostly dissolved, so the silence is weaker evidence than it sounds. Nomads leave almost nothing for a spade to find, which is why the empty Sinai cannot carry the weight placed on it. Excavations in the eastern Nile delta have uncovered large Semitic populations settled exactly where Exodus puts the Hebrews. Exodus 1:11 names the store city Raamses, matching Pi-Ramesses, the capital built in the thirteenth century BC and later abandoned, a detail hard to explain if the story were invented centuries afterward in Judah. The Egyptologist Kenneth Kitchen has catalogued such background fits at length, from brick quotas to the treaty form of the covenant. And by about 1208 BC the Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian victory inscription, already names Israel as a people in Canaan. Israel came from somewhere.

The field is genuinely split, and the split often follows prior assumptions about what the text is allowed to be. Scholars also debate the date, an earlier reading built on 1 Kings 6:1 against a thirteenth-century setting, and the scale, since the Hebrew word usually rendered thousand may in some texts mean clan, which would shrink the marching numbers considerably.

What nobody disputes is where Israel anchored its memory. The creed of the wandering Aramean, the Passover, the prophets, the psalms, all treat the exodus as the founding fact. Ancient peoples invented glorious origins for themselves. Slavery is a strange glory to invent.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians who trust the account still differ on its date, scale, and route, and on how much weight archaeology should carry in reading Scripture at all. Advocates of full inerrancy expect text and trowel to converge and read the delta evidence as steady vindication. Others hold the account as true covenant memory told in the idiom of ancient narrative and are unbothered by open questions of number and geography. Nearly all agree on method, that absence of evidence in a nomadic desert context is weak evidence of absence, and that patience has repeatedly been rewarded in this field, where cities and peoples once called legendary have turned up under the sand.

questions.question: What do I do with the psalms that curse people?
questions.shortAnswer: Do not sand them down. They are the prayers of the brutalized handing vengeance to God instead of taking it, and they are in your Bible partly so that rage has somewhere holy to go.
questions.answer:
Psalm 137 ends with a blessing on whoever seizes Babylonian infants and dashes them against the rock. There is no reading of that verse that makes it comfortable, and you should distrust anyone who smooths it quickly. C. S. Lewis, who loved the Psalms, wrote that the hatred in them strikes the reader in the face like heat from a furnace. If your first reaction is horror, your conscience is working.

Now look closely at what these prayers are and are not. They are not commands, and they are not policy. No one in Psalm 137 is ordered to do anything. They are the poetry of the violated, exiles who had watched exactly that horror done to their own children by Babylon's army, saying the unspeakable to God instead of doing it to someone. The address is the point. The psalm hands the case to the only court left. Vengeance is mine, I will repay, the Lord had said, and the imprecatory psalms are what taking that promise seriously sounds like from the gutter. The alternative to praying your rage is not having none. It is nursing it, or acting on it.

The New Testament does not delete these psalms. Peter quotes two of them about Judas. Jesus dies with a psalm on his lips, and the martyrs under the altar in Revelation still cry out, how long before you judge? What changes in Christ is the direction of hope. God's enemies now have an offer on the table, and the church is commanded to bless its persecutors while still trusting God to judge. Both notes stand together. A God who will never judge evil is not good news to anyone who has lived underneath evil.

So pray them the way the church at its best always has, with the psalmist's honesty and the crucified Lord in view, aimed at the real enemies, sin and death and the powers behind them, and at human evil handed wholly over to the Judge who does all things right.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Some traditions keep every imprecatory line in the psalter and pray them corporately, arguing that Scripture gives them for use, not for display. Others hold that Christians may no longer pray them against persons after the command to love enemies, and instead read them as prophecy of God's judgment or pray them only against evil itself. Some lectionaries omit the hardest verses from public reading, and other Christians think that omission teaches the church a false gentility. Nearly all agree on two things, that the abused may pray their honesty without shame, and that the same Bible binds the church to enemy-love.

questions.question: Why did God command animal sacrifice?
questions.shortAnswer: Not because he needed feeding. The system taught, in blood and cost, what sin actually is, and it was designed from the start to be outgrown, which is exactly what the New Testament says happened.
questions.answer:
To modern readers the sacrificial system looks primitive and cruel, rivers of blood to appease an offended deity. Do not rush past that reaction, because Scripture itself refuses the pagan version of the idea. The nations around Israel fed their gods, who were hungry. Israel's God says the opposite in so many words. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine. Whatever the altars were for, they were not for God's benefit. And the prophets thunder against sacrifice offered as a transaction, Hosea insisting that God desires steadfast love and not sacrifice. The system's own Scriptures relativize the system. That is the first clue that something else is going on.

What was going on was teaching of the costliest kind. Leviticus 17:11 gives the logic in one line. The life of the flesh is in the blood, and it is given on the altar to make atonement. Sin, the system taught, is not an etiquette violation. It costs life. Every worshiper who pressed a hand onto the animal's head learned in the nerves, not just the mind, that forgiveness is never free, that something dies when a person sins, and that God himself had provided a substitute so the sinner could walk home alive. You could not leave the tabernacle believing sin was small.

And the letter to the Hebrews insists the system said one more thing by its sheer repetition. It never finished. The same animals, morning after morning, year after year, because the blood of bulls and goats cannot finally take away sins. The altars were a signpost that ached toward something beyond themselves. When John the Baptist saw Jesus and announced the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, a thousand years of imagery snapped into place. The system ended, Christians believe, not because it was false but because it was fulfilled, one sacrifice for sins for all time.

So read Leviticus the way you would read a tutor. Strange, exacting, bloody, and aimed the whole time at the cross.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians agree the sacrifices pointed to Christ and differ on the mechanics of what his death accomplished. Substitutionary readings put the Levitical logic of exchange at the center. Christus Victor readings stress the defeat of sin, death, and the powers. Moral influence readings stress the love the cross reveals and awakens. Most traditions hold these together rather than choosing one. They also differ on how directly each Levitical detail maps onto Calvary, some finding Christ in every fold of the tabernacle curtains, others content with the broad strokes Hebrews itself draws.

questions.question: Why do Christians ignore some Old Testament laws and quote others?
questions.shortAnswer: The shellfish argument lands on Christians who quote Leviticus carelessly, and it should. The actual answer is about covenant, not cherry-picking, and the New Testament does the sorting in the open.
questions.answer:
The objection usually arrives with a smirk, but it deserves a straight face, because it names a real inconsistency. A Christian who quotes Leviticus at a neighbor while eating shrimp and wearing blended fabric owes somebody an explanation, and church history includes people wielding the law selectively as a weapon. If Christians treat the Old Testament as a menu, the critic is right to say so.

But the Christian claim was never that the law is a menu. It is that the law was a covenant, a whole national constitution given to Israel for a particular era of the story, and that Christians relate to it through Christ, who said he came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it. Fulfillment is the load-bearing word. A promissory note is not ignored when it is paid. The food laws, the sacrifices, the festival calendar, the purity code existed to mark Israel out among the nations and to point forward. And the New Testament retires them in the open, on the record, with reasons given. Jesus declares all foods clean in Mark 7. The apostles in Acts 15 formally decline to place the law's yoke on gentile converts. Hebrews explains at length why the sacrifices ended. Nobody is sneaking anything off the list.

What carries over is what the New Testament itself re-teaches. The commands against murder, adultery, theft, and false witness all reappear, and beneath them the two on which Jesus said everything hangs, love of God and love of neighbor. Later theologians sorted the law into moral, ceremonial, and civil aspects to systematize this, and while some scholars find those categories tidier than the text, the instinct behind them is apostolic. Paul can write that circumcision counts for nothing and that keeping the commandments of God counts, in the same letter, without contradicting himself.

So the sorting principle is public and consistent. Not which laws we happen to like, but which commands the new covenant renews, which it fulfills, and which it retires, with the reasons stated where anyone can read them.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The frameworks differ on the machinery. Covenant theology reads one covenant of grace across both testaments and keeps the moral law, summarized in the Ten Commandments, as the abiding rule of Christian life. Dispensationalism draws a sharper line at the cross and treats the Mosaic code as a completed administration. Progressive covenantalism and new covenant theology argue that Christians are bound to the law of Christ rather than to Moses as such, with the Sabbath command as the classic test case. These are second-order and third-order differences among people who agree that the ceremonial law is fulfilled and that love of God and neighbor binds forever.

questions.question: If I had been born in another country, wouldn't I believe another religion?
questions.shortAnswer: Probably, and that fact should humble every believer. But an argument about where beliefs come from cannot tell you whether they are true, and it disarms the skeptic's own convictions just as fast.
questions.answer:
Take the observation seriously, because it is simply true. Religious belief tracks geography and family. A child born in Riyadh will likely pray as a Muslim, a child born in Tibet as a Buddhist, and a great deal of Christian confidence is plain inheritance. If that thought has never unsettled you, you have not sat with it long enough. It should make every believer slower to sneer at the sincere faith of others, since sincerity is distributed evenly across the map.

But watch what the argument does when you let it run. It applies to every conviction, not only the religious ones. A person born in eleventh-century Mongolia would not have believed in universal human rights, and a person born in Copenhagen today probably does. If demographic predictability discredits a belief, it discredits the skeptic's beliefs at exactly the same rate. The truth is that where a belief comes from and whether it is true are separate questions, and confusing them has a name in logic, the genetic fallacy. You believe arithmetic because of where and when you were schooled. It is still true.

So the map cannot settle the question. It has to be settled the ordinary way, by weighing the claims. Christianity makes a peculiar one, that God acted in public history, in a Roman province, in a man who was executed and then, his followers testified at the cost of their lives, seen alive. That claim is true or false for everyone, Danish or Saudi, and it invites investigation rather than inheritance. It is also worth noticing that the faith has never stayed inside its birth demographics. It began Jewish, became mostly gentile, and its center of gravity now sits in Africa, Asia, and Latin America, among first-generation believers who were, by the accident-of-birth logic, supposed to be something else.

And Scripture already thought of this. Paul told the Athenians that God fixed the boundaries of every nation's dwelling so that they should seek him and perhaps find him, for he is not far from any one of us. The map, in that telling, is not a cage. It is a starting point.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians divide over what this means for those who never hear the gospel, a question a related entry treats at length. Exclusivists hold that salvation comes through explicit faith in Christ wherever the message reaches. Inclusivists hold that Christ's work can reach people who responded to the light they were given. All the historic traditions agree on two things, that God's final judgment will be recognizably just, and that no one gets to redraw the map of God's mercy, wider or narrower, with more confidence than Scripture gives.

questions.question: Didn't Christianity just copy older dying-and-rising god myths?
questions.shortAnswer: The parallels shrink dramatically on inspection, and it was the scholars of myth who shrank them. The resurrection claim is Jewish, datable, and tied to named people, which is not how myths behave.
questions.answer:
The theory deserves its day, because it was once serious scholarship. James Frazer's The Golden Bough, published in 1890, gathered gods who die and return, Osiris, Tammuz, Adonis, and a generation concluded that the Jesus story was one more seasonal myth in Jewish dress. Christians should also concede the adjacent facts cheerfully. December 25 was chosen centuries later and owes something to the Roman calendar, and the church has absorbed and baptized customs from every culture it entered. If the claim is that Christianity's packaging carries pagan fingerprints, the claim is true.

But the copying theory itself collapsed inside the academy, and religion scholars did the demolition. Examined case by case, the parallels blur. Osiris does not rise. He becomes lord of the dead below. Tammuz's return is a seasonal cycle, not a claim about a man in history. The Mithras sometimes advertised as a resurrected rival was born from a rock, and most of the evidence for his cult postdates the New Testament. Jonathan Z. Smith, no friend of apologetics, argued that the whole dying-and-rising category dissolves under inspection. Vegetation cycles and underworld myths are simply a different kind of thing from a dated execution under a named governor.

And the resurrection claim behaves nothing like myth in its form. It is tied to a specific Passover, a named tomb owner, and named living witnesses. The summary Paul hands on in 1 Corinthians 15, that Christ died, was buried, was raised, and appeared to Cephas and the twelve and five hundred at once, is dated by most scholars, skeptical ones included, to within a few years of the crucifixion. Myths thicken over centuries. This was a checkable claim circulating while the witnesses could still be questioned, in a Jewish culture that had no category for one man rising in the middle of history. As Paul said at his trial, this was not done in a corner.

Resemblance, it turns out, was never the same thing as ancestry.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians differ on what to make of the genuine echoes. Some, following C. S. Lewis's idea of myth become fact, read pagan longing as God-planted preparation, so the old stories are friendly witnesses to a hunger the gospel answers. Others prefer stark contrast and see in the myths only human religion at its most inventive. There are also family debates about celebrating festivals with mixed histories, which most traditions settle by asking what a practice means now rather than where a date came from. On the central point there is no divide. The resurrection is confessed as history, not as a metaphor for spring.

questions.question: Why does God demand worship? Isn't that vanity?
questions.shortAnswer: If God needed our praise, it would be. The Christian claim is stranger, that worship is commanded for the worshiper's sake, the way a doctor commands food, because delighting in the highest good is what health looks like.
questions.answer:
State the objection at full strength, because it has teeth. Christopher Hitchens liked to describe heaven as a celestial dictatorship, an eternity of compulsory praise for a ruler who cannot get enough of it. In a human being we would call the craving for constant admiration a disorder. And the church has sometimes made the charge easier, singing to God as though he were an insecure king who needed managing. If that were the claim, the objection would win.

The actual doctrine cuts the legs from under it. Christian theology has always taught what it calls aseity, that God lacks nothing and draws life from nothing outside himself. Paul says it flatly in Athens, that God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. A being who needs no worship cannot be vain for commanding it. So the command must be doing something else, and the question is what.

C. S. Lewis found the answer while fighting this very objection. He noticed that praise is what enjoyment does when it is healthy. Lovers praise the beloved, hikers the view, readers the book, and the praise is not flattery. It is the joy completing itself, the delight running over into words. Now run that logic upward. If God is the supreme good, the fountain every lesser joy runs from, then commanding worship is not demanding tribute. It is prescribing the one activity in which a creature's joy comes fully alive. In your presence there is fullness of joy, says the psalm. The command to worship is the command to be where the joy is.

There is a darker angle too. Human beings never stop worshiping. They only change objects, money, nation, romance, the self, and every one of those gods devours its devotees. The first commandment, read this way, is a protection order. God insists on being worshiped partly because he is the only object of worship that will not eat you.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians agree that God needs nothing and differ over worship's proper shape. Reformed churches historically hold the regulative principle, that public worship includes only what Scripture commands. Lutherans, Anglicans, and most free churches follow the normative principle, allowing what Scripture does not forbid. Traditions also weigh form differently, from fixed liturgy and sacrament to spontaneity and song, and they argue in-house about whether contemporary worship culture forms joy or performs it. None of those debates touch the floor beneath them, that worship is for God's glory and the creature's good at once, and never for God's need.

questions.question: Is God male?
questions.shortAnswer: No. God is spirit, beyond the categories he created, and Scripture says so plainly. It also gives the language he chose for himself, Father and Son alongside the Bible's own mother imagery, and the church keeps both facts.
questions.answer:
Begin with the wound that usually sits under the question. The church has often talked as if God were a man, and as if men were therefore a little more like God, and both moves have been used to diminish women. If you have met that, your suspicion is earned. The correction, though, does not come from modern sensitivity. It comes from the Bible's own doctrine of God.

Scripture is blunt that God is not a creature and has no body. God is spirit, Jesus says. God is not a man, says Numbers. I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst, says Hosea. And the Bible's first chapter makes the decisive statement. God created humanity in his own image, male and female he created them. Both sexes image God. Neither is the closer likeness. Whatever maleness is, God is not it, and the great theologians of every century, long before anyone accused them of a modern agenda, said exactly this. The catechisms still do, teaching that God is neither man nor woman.

Yet the same Bible reaches for feminine imagery without embarrassment. God comforts as a mother comforts her child, cries out like a woman in labor, remembers his people like a nursing mother who could never forget her baby, and Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem the way a hen gathers her brood under her wings. The imagery runs both directions because God is the source of both. What Scripture does not do is address God as Mother or name him goddess, and the church has largely held that line, not because the feminine is lesser but because Jesus gave his people a particular address. When you pray, he said, say Father. Christians did not choose that name, and most have not felt free to improve on it. It is revelation's given name, not biology's category.

So the answer has two hands, and you need both. God is beyond sex. And God has given his name. Keeping the first without the second loses the Bible's God for an abstraction. Keeping the second without the first turns him into a big man in the sky, which is its own idolatry.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The live debate concerns language in prayer and liturgy. Some mainline Protestants revise or supplement Father language in worship, arguing that exclusively masculine address wounds and misleads. Catholic, Orthodox, and most evangelical churches keep the biblical names while affirming with the catechisms that God transcends sex, and they argue that renaming God trades revelation for our own projections. There are quieter in-house conversations as well, about how to speak of the Spirit and about recovering the Bible's own maternal imagery in preaching, which nearly everyone agrees the church has underused.

questions.question: If the Holy Spirit guides Christians, why do they disagree so much?
questions.shortAnswer: Because the promised guidance was never a promised bypass of human finitude and sin. Look closer and the disagreement has a shape, wide at the edges, strikingly narrow at the center.
questions.answer:
The objection practically writes itself. Jesus promised that the Spirit of truth would guide his people into all truth, and his people have divided into more traditions than anyone can neatly count, disagreeing about baptism, the Supper, the end times, and plenty in between. If one teacher guided every reader, you would expect the readings to converge. The point lands, and Christians should feel its weight rather than hurry past it.

Three honest observations follow. First, read John 16 in its setting. The promise was spoken to the apostles in the upper room, and the church has always heard its primary fulfillment in the apostolic witness itself, the New Testament, not in a private data feed to every believer. The Spirit's ongoing work is real, illumination, conviction, comfort, but Scripture nowhere promises that regenerate people become infallible readers. Second, the Spirit guides the willing, and the church's divisions have rarely featured two humble parties beyond pride's reach. Paul told the quarreling Corinthians that their factions proved they were still of the flesh. Some disagreement is honest finitude. A grievous amount is us, and the Spirit gets blamed for what pride accomplished.

Third, and least noticed, look at the actual shape of the disagreement. It is wide at the edges and narrow at the center. The churches that fight about the millennium and the mode of baptism confess, across every continent and century, the same creed, one God, Father, Son, and Spirit, Christ crucified and risen, forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body. That convergence, among rivals who could never have coordinated it, is easy to stop seeing. Where the faith itself is at stake, the line has held for two thousand years. The family arguments over second things are real, and this site takes them seriously, but they are arguments inside a shared house.

The command that remains is Paul's, to be eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Eager is a working word. Unity was never promised as automatic. It was assigned.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: There is even a disagreement about the disagreement. Catholics and Orthodox hold that the Spirit guides the church through its councils, tradition, and teaching office, and that Protestant division is the predictable cost of setting that instrument aside. Protestants answer that councils and popes have erred, that Scripture must stay free to correct the church, and that the shared confession of separated churches shows the Spirit was never confined to one chair. Cessationists and continuationists differ further over how the Spirit's guidance operates in the present day. The doctrine page on the Spirit lays out that terrain fairly.
