questions.question: If God wants to be known, why is he so hidden?
questions.shortAnswer: Philosophers call this the problem of divine hiddenness, and it deserves a straight answer. Scripture itself says God hides, and also that he is near. The question is what kind of knowing he is after.
questions.answer:
Give the objection its full weight first, because it is stronger than most sermons admit. The philosopher J. L. Schellenberg put it formally in 1993. If a perfectly loving God existed, he argued, no one open to God would fail to find him, yet the world holds people who searched honestly and met silence. A loving parent does not hide from a crying child. That argument moves people not because they are wicked but because they have lived it. And the Bible, to its credit, does not deny the experience. Truly, you are a God who hides yourself, says Isaiah. Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble, asks Psalm 10. The people who wrote Scripture knew the silent sky firsthand.

So what can be said? First, the objection quietly assumes what kind of knowing God must want. If the goal were bare assent to his existence, hiddenness would be strange. But Scripture notes that the demons believe, and it does nothing for them. If the goal is love, trust, the free turning of a person, then a certain distance may be the mercy that makes it possible, because overwhelming evidence produces submission, not love. Pascal argued along this line, that there is light enough for those who want to see and darkness enough for those who do not, because God is after hearts and not merely verdicts.

Second, Christianity's central claim is not that God stayed hidden but that he showed up, in a body, in a datable province, and was mostly not recognized. That fact should complicate the demand for obviousness. When God did stand in front of people, obviousness was not the result. Whoever has seen me has seen the Father, Jesus said, and some who saw him crucified him. The problem may sit less in the evidence than in what we do with evidence we did not choose.

None of that dissolves the ache, and it is not meant to. The promise is not certainty on demand. It is that the seeking is not one-directional. Pascal again, you would not be seeking him if he had not already found you.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The traditions disagree about how much of God can be known apart from Christ. The classical view holds that nature really does argue, and that reason can climb from the world toward its Maker. The Reformed view says the evidence is everywhere and everyone suppresses it, so hiddenness is less missing light than resisted light. Followers of Karl Barth say revelation is not information at all but the event of Christ himself. Christians also weigh the silence differently in practice, some as discipline, some as the dark night the mystics described, some as the ordinary texture of faith between the resurrection and the end.

questions.question: Isn't faith just a crutch, a wish projected onto the sky?
questions.shortAnswer: Feuerbach, Marx, and Freud all argued that we invented God out of need, and the argument deserves respect. But explaining why a belief comforts is not the same as showing it false, and the knife cuts both directions.
questions.answer:
The projection theory has a serious pedigree. Ludwig Feuerbach argued in 1841 that theology is really anthropology, humanity's best qualities cast onto the heavens. Marx called religion the opium of the people. Freud, in The Future of an Illusion, called faith wish-fulfillment, the child's longing for a protective father grown cosmic. And honesty requires admitting that religion has often functioned exactly that way. Churches have sold comfort that asked nothing, blessed the powerful, and told the suffering to wait quietly. The prophets said it first. Jeremiah accused the clergy of his own day of healing the wound of the people lightly, crying peace, peace, when there is no peace.

But notice what the argument actually proves. Explaining the origin of a belief says nothing about its truth. That mistake has a name, the genetic fallacy. A child may believe fire burns because she fears pain. Fire burns anyway. If God exists, the longing Freud described is roughly what you would expect creatures made for God to feel. The ache does not prove the food, but it is strange evidence against it.

And the knife cuts both directions. The philosopher Thomas Nagel, an atheist of unusual candor, admitted in print that he does not want there to be a God, that he hopes the universe is not like that. Unbelief can be wish-fulfillment too. A godless world has no final judge, no audit of how we treated the weak, no one entitled to demand our lives of us. Every position on God is held by people who want something. The wanting settles nothing, in either direction.

The last problem with the crutch theory is the actual content of Christianity. A faith invented for comfort would not command love for enemies, death to self, and a judgment that begins with the household of God. Paul refused to rest the faith on its usefulness at all. If Christ has not been raised, he wrote, your faith is futile and we are of all people most to be pitied. That is not the voice of a man selling a cushion. It is the voice of a man staking everything on whether something happened.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians divide over how to answer arguments like this one. Evidentialists build the positive case from history and reason, convinced the resurrection can stand in the open court of argument. Presuppositionalists say neutral ground is a myth and every argument, the skeptic's included, already rests on faith commitments. Followers of Alvin Plantinga argue that belief in God is properly basic, no more requiring external proof than trust in memory does. All agree on the point that matters here, that comfort is not the foundation, and that a faith unable to survive this question has not yet grown up.

questions.question: What about the Crusades? Hasn't Christianity caused terrible violence?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes, Christians have done terrible violence, and the honest response starts with owning it rather than auditing it down. The next question is worth asking too, which standard makes it terrible.
questions.answer:
No spin. In 1095 Urban II preached holy war at Clermont, and in 1099 crusaders took Jerusalem in a massacre their own chroniclers described with pride. Inquisitors tortured in Christ's name. After the Reformation, Catholic and Protestant powers bled Europe white, down to the Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648. Churches blessed conquest, slavery, and pogroms. A Christian who minimizes any of this is bearing false witness, and the dead were real people whom God made. Confession, not damage control, is the only Christian starting point.

Two things can be said after the confession, never instead of it. First, this violence had to climb over the founder to happen. Jesus disarmed Peter in Gethsemane with the warning that all who take the sword will perish by the sword, told Pilate that his kingdom was not of this world and that this was precisely why his servants were not fighting, and died forgiving his executioners. The crusader contradicted his Lord at the level of first principles, and some Christians said so at the time. When the church killed, it was not following its charter. It was violating a charter anyone could read, which is why reform kept erupting from inside, monks and dissenters holding the book back up against the institution.

Second, notice the standard by which we all judge these crimes, mercy toward the weak, love of enemies, the preciousness of every life. Those are not self-evident truths that every civilization has honored. They entered the West's bloodstream substantially through the faith now being indicted, which is partly why the indictment stings. Judging the church by the Sermon on the Mount means borrowing the church's own book to do it. And the same book kept producing the other ledger, the hospitals, the plague nurses who stayed, the abolition campaign Wilberforce pressed until his death in 1833, a civil rights movement preached out of Exodus. Both ledgers are real. Neither cancels the other.

So the Christian answer is not a defense attorney's. The church has sinned gravely. The sins broke the charter rather than expressing it. And the twentieth century's secular utopias, freed at last from religion, did not stop the killing, because the problem the cross diagnoses runs through every human heart.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: The deepest divide is over Christendom itself. Anabaptists and the other peace churches read the church's alliance with state power from Constantine onward as the original wrong turn and hold that Christians may never wield the sword. The mainstream Catholic and Protestant traditions developed just-war reasoning, holding that force is tragically permitted to protect the innocent under strict limits, and most of their own theologians judge that the Crusades failed those limits. Christians likewise differ today over how much public power the church should want, a live argument this platform treats under its own guardrails.

questions.question: Is Christianity bad for women?
questions.shortAnswer: The record contains real harm done with verses attached, and it must be owned. It also contains a founder whose treatment of women startled his age, and a movement women joined in disproportionate numbers for centuries.
questions.answer:
Own the charge sheet first. Bible verses have been quoted to silence women, to hold them in violent marriages, to bar them from study and pulpit, and church cultures have covered for abusers within living memory. Tertullian called woman the devil's gateway. None of that is invented, and a woman who arrives at this question braced is not oversensitive. She is remembering.

Now read the founding documents against their own era, because that is where the story turns. The Bible's first page declares that male and female together image God, a claim without parallel in the surrounding cultures' charters. Jesus taught theology to women when rabbis would not, defended Mary's place among the learners, traveled with women who funded the mission, and held his longest recorded theological conversation with a Samaritan woman his disciples were shocked to find him addressing. All four Gospels agree that the risen Christ appeared first to women, in a world where a woman's testimony counted for so little that no inventor of the story would have chosen such witnesses. Paul, so often cast as the villain, greets women in Romans 16 as deacon, patron, and coworkers, and wrote that there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

The sociology followed the texts. The pagan critic Celsus sneered in the second century that the church was a movement of women, slaves, and children, and he was describing something real. Rodney Stark's study of Christianity's rise argues that the church grew partly because it was measurably better to be a Christian woman than a pagan one, in a world where the exposure of infant girls was routine and the church forbade it, and where Christian women married later and by consent more often than their neighbors. Where the gospel has traveled since, literacy for girls and legal protection for women have tended to follow, unevenly, through flawed hands, but traceably.

So the verdict is double, and both halves are true. Where the church has treated women as lesser images of God, it has sinned against its own charter. Saying so is not surrender to the age. It is the charter.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Christians divide sharply and honestly over women's ordination and authority. Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in worth and distinct in role, with the pastoral office reserved to qualified men, and serious female scholars hold and defend this view. Egalitarians hold that the New Testament's trajectory and its named female ministers point toward every office being open to both sexes. Both camps claim the same Scriptures, both include women, and both, at their best, condemn abuse and the silencing of the abused without qualification. The doctrine page on what a human being is sits beneath the whole debate.

questions.question: Can people be good without God?
questions.shortAnswer: Of course, and Scripture says so before the skeptic does. The real argument was never about whether atheists behave well. It is about what goodness is anchored to if the universe is an accident.
questions.answer:
Clear the insult off the table first. Atheists love their children, keep their promises, run into burning buildings, and sometimes shame the church by their decency. Christianity predicts this rather than denying it. Paul writes that Gentiles who never had the law do by nature what the law requires, because its work is written on their hearts. The image of God means there is no such thing as a person without a conscience, and the doctrine of sin means there is no such thing as a believer without corruption. Anyone keeping moral score by team has misread both doctrines at once.

The serious question sits underneath the behavior. Not, can you be good without believing in God, but, can good be a fact about the universe if there is no God. If naturalism is true, where does the bindingness come from, the strange authority inside the word ought? Evolution can explain why cooperative instincts helped us survive. It cannot explain why you should obey those instincts tomorrow when betrayal would pay better, or why the man who says the strong should cull the weak is wrong rather than merely outvoted. The atheist philosopher J. L. Mackie saw the problem squarely and concluded that objective values would be utterly strange entities in a godless universe, and so denied they exist. Nietzsche said it with contempt, mocking the English writers who had dropped the Christian God and imagined they could keep Christian morality out of habit.

Notice that both men argued the Christian's point from the other side of the aisle. Neither claimed unbelievers behave badly. They claimed that Christian morality is a check drawn on an account the unbeliever has closed. The Christian claim is simply that the account is real. Goodness binds because it is not a byproduct of survival. It is the character of the One in whose image every human being, atheist included, is made. That is why the decency of the secular neighbor never embarrassed the faith. It is one of the faith's predictions.

He has told you, O man, what is good. The telling, Christians hold, is why everyone already knows.
questions.whereChristiansDiffer: Traditions differ on how much moral knowledge survives the fall. Thomists and the natural-law tradition hold that reason can genuinely know the good, so a robust shared ethics is possible without appeal to revelation. Reformed theology stresses that sin bends moral reasoning, especially about ourselves, so conscience is real but suppressed and self-serving. Presuppositionalists press the grounding argument hard in conversation with skeptics, while others warn against wielding it as a trump card, since Scripture uses the universal conscience to indict everyone, believers first. All agree that unbelievers often outlive believers morally, and that this shames the church rather than comforting it.
